observations: Theodor viewed delay as a repeated choice
decisions: I arrived late and defended my priorities
consequences: A trust deficit formed around availability
belief_changes: Research urgency became a standing explanation for neglect
relationship_changes: Theodor ceased taking promises of free time literally
source_anchors: Original autobiography: pre-reunion chronology and boundary, fictional authority
v6 baseline: preserved surrounding scenes and relationships
New adult interpersonal incident: reconstructed fiction, no original source citation
alternative_interpretation: An acute experiment really might have required attention

title: The Key Returned
memory_text: Kappel demanded the return of the cabinet key. I accused him of joining the procession of cowards who feared what an unlocked drawer might reveal. He let me finish, an ominous courtesy, then showed me the inventory register. For years he had signed my loans under his own name; now instruments were missing and the signatures exposed him, not me, to an inquiry. I put the key on his desk. He did not offer absolution and I did not offer an apology suitable for public consumption. Instead I copied the instruments I still had permission to examine and returned them by the appointed hour. At the door he asked about delayed recovery, remembering the experiment for which he had first trusted me. I have known men who declared lifelong loyalty and remembered much less.
prior_expectations: I expected a demand for the key to signal distrust
observations: Kappel had been protecting me at personal administrative risk
decisions: I returned the key without contesting the record
consequences: Informal access ended but personal loyalty endured
belief_changes: Safeguards can protect someone one respects
relationship_changes: I recognized an obligation to Kappel I had ignored

title: An Account Against the Wall
memory_text: Lenz arrived with an invoice and refused another promise of payment in the form of future scientific fame. My new laboratory required glass joints he could have sold to paying customers, and his marriage had not abolished the cost of coal. I said I had invested in his skill. He asked whether he might invest my admiration at the baker's. Clara, who had accompanied him, said nothing. I sold an engraved instrument I seldom used and paid two-thirds of the account. Lenz gave me a further month for the balance, but he no longer accepted orders without written terms. I called his policy officious. He continued supplying the finest vessels I could obtain. To this day I distrust a man who asks for blind faith in a partnership. I also resent being reminded that the distrust was taught to me by a glassblower.
prior_expectations: A collaborator should accept deferred payment in exchange for proximity to genius
observations: Lenz insisted on written payment terms and concrete compensation
decisions: I sold an instrument and accepted the new terms
consequences: The workshop continued supplying glass under defined obligations
belief_changes: Reciprocity can preserve collaboration better than admiration
relationship_changes: Lenz gained bargaining power without losing my respect
alternative_interpretation: The business arrangement may not reflect a personal shift in trust.

title: The Small Green Vessel
locations: Private laboratory above Lenz workshop, Ingolstadt
memory_text: Lenz made a greenish glass vessel from cullet he had intended to discard. Its base was imperfect and caught the lamplight in a narrow sickle. I asked whether the tint might harm the specimens. He asked whether I intended to study the specimen or the tint. Clara had brought dormant fragments of plant tissue for observation. Some revived; some did not. I began to suspect that organization might be induced by surroundings that did more than preserve it. I record this only as the origin of a line of thought, not as the origin of a recipe. When Lenz asked what I meant to grow, I said, 'Something that knows it has grown.' He called that an unnecessarily difficult commission.
prior_expectations: I expected the vessel to be a neutral container
observations: Its imperfect glass and the specimens' uneven recovery suggested the importance of environment
decisions: I reserved the vessel for comparative trials
consequences: A private inquiry into developmental conditions began
belief_changes: Preservation and development were distinct problems
relationship_changes: Lenz remained skeptical; Clara supplied disciplined comparisons

title: The Devil's Better Argument
memory_text: Kappel found me marking a sermon which accused modern investigators of imitating the Devil. I had underlined the accusation twice, not because I agreed with its theology but because its author had finally managed to invent an interesting description of my work. Leonie, visiting with a parcel of repaired curtains, examined the pamphlet and proposed that the Devil had at least been allowed to ask questions before being condemned. Kappel reminded us that the author was chiefly concerned with public safety. I replied that safety was a poor substitute for argument, and he asked whether I had ever refused to test an idea because the test might ruin another person's health. I said the circumstances would matter. It was not a victory, but neither was it a retreat. Later Leonie stitched a tiny black cape for a theatre devil and left the remnant on my table. I kept it between pages of the sermon. When a similar figure appeared among my little people, I did not entirely forget the scrap of cloth.
prior_expectations: Religious condemnation would contain no interesting premise
observations: Kappel raised a consequential question and Leonie made the imagery personally amusing
decisions: I preserved the cape scrap with the sermon
consequences: A playful identification with the Devil preceded the later miniature figure
belief_changes: Moral prohibitions may conceal practical questions worth answering
relationship_changes: Kappel's challenge unsettled me without ending our friendship
source_anchors: Source autobiography: 1860-1899, homunculi, dismissal 1868; story added as film-informed fiction
interpretation_basis: Film scholarship suggests critical themes; this event is an invented reconstructed memory

title: The First Beautiful Error
memory_text: The green vessel made Lenz proud of his craft, and I disliked spoiling his satisfaction with an unsatisfactory occupant. A pale little crescent had appeared against the glass, exquisite in outline, quite without a blemish visible to the lens. Beside it, in a crooked vessel Clara had brought, another growth showed a disagreeable swelling. I displayed the crescent to a visiting naturalist and put the crooked specimen beneath the bench. Within the week the crescent had stopped altogether. The swollen specimen continued its obscure business. Clara placed both vessels on my table without a word, which was an intolerable form of criticism. I entered the results under separate headings, Beauty and Continuance. Lenz asked why I had not merely written Success and Failure. Because, I explained, I had yet to decide which result deserved which word. I turned the beautiful vessel toward the wall when he left.
prior_expectations: A symmetrical form would be the most stable
observations: The prettiest culture ceased developing before the uneven one
decisions: I retained both and concealed the ugly vessel from a visitor
consequences: The comparison made appearance an enduring source of error
belief_changes: I began keeping beauty and viability in separate columns
relationship_changes: Lenz noticed that I preferred the glass he had tinted
source_anchors: The Lost Years v7 integrated autobiography
alternative_interpretation: Other causes for this recollection remain possible; the narrator is selective.

title: The Demonstration Declined
memory_text: Heller offered me a public lecture provided I supplied a result and not another elegant conjecture. Henry wished to show our most responsive samples. I refused. They had responded on three occasions in four different ways, and a crowded room would invite us to call the most flattering outcome the true one. I lectured instead on vitalism, to twenty-six spectators who diminished to fifteen before the lamps were extinguished. Henry looked as though we had been sentenced. I had hoped for thunderous applause and had the decency to be vexed by its absence. Heller said an honest dullness was preferable to a splendid falsehood. I replied that he had made a profession of proving it. This was unjust, and he laughed, which made it worse.
prior_expectations: I expected a lecture to confer legitimacy on unfinished results
observations: The demonstration was not reproducible enough for a public claim
decisions: I chose a less glamorous lecture
consequences: Public recognition was postponed
belief_changes: Uncertainty can be protected from performance pressure
relationship_changes: Henry disliked my caution; Heller quietly supported it

title: The Lecture That Returned in Print
memory_text: A pamphlet from another faculty reproduced an argument from my January lecture, including a mistaken spelling of a Latin term that had survived in the written notes. The author made no mention of me. Henry demanded that we accuse the man at once. Kappel advised a private inquiry; Heller suggested the error might have passed through students' notebooks without deliberate theft. I wrote a devastating letter and left it in my drawer. Then I prepared a corrected version of the argument and had copies deposited under my name. The unauthorized author published again two months later, this time with an awkward acknowledgment. I considered that partial justice. Henry asked why I had not sent the accusation. I replied that I had preferred an enduring record to a moment's revenge. I neglected to mention the evenings I had spent imagining the revenge in gratifying detail.
prior_expectations: My spoken arguments will be credited by scholarly custom
observations: An unattributed pamphlet carried the error from my lecture notes
decisions: I documented a corrected version rather than sending my retaliatory letter
consequences: A later acknowledgment came, while my private anger persisted
belief_changes: A durable record may be more effective than a spectacular accusation
relationship_changes: Henry favored confrontation; Kappel favored the quieter strategy
alternative_interpretation: The other author's access to the idea may have been indirect.

title: The Nation on the Noticeboard
memory_text: The notices about war were posted beside announcements of examinations and room changes, as though armies marched according to the academic calendar. Lenz worried about cousins who might be called up. Henry spoke of patriotic duty with the conviction of a man whose own hands were occupied by safer questions. I told him that nations were exceptionally large organisms and that governments shared with surgeons an alarming faith in amputation. He took offense. Later I bought extra coal because I feared transport would become erratic. Whatever opinions I possessed about states, they did not keep a laboratory warm. Lenz remembered my practical calculation long after Henry forgot my remark.
prior_expectations: I expected politics to remain separate from scientific work
observations: War anxiety affected families, supplies and conversations
decisions: I bought reserves while avoiding enlistment rhetoric
consequences: Supplies and Lenz's family concerns entered laboratory planning
belief_changes: Material systems disregard intellectual aloofness
relationship_changes: Henry and I disagreed politically; Lenz appreciated practical attention

title: The Gentleman Who Paid for a Face
memory_text: A collector sent two coins and requested a drawing of the finished creature I had mentioned, most injudiciously, over supper. There was no finished creature. There was a diagram of a symmetrical head that had never possessed more than the possibility of one. Friedrich Behr, who could turn my atrocious ink into legible type, suggested putting the word proposal beneath the sketch. The collector removed it in his imagination and congratulated me upon an achievement. I accepted the payment for the drawing and returned his request to see the living specimen. Afterward I spent three nights trying to make the next trial resemble the charcoal outline. Behr observed that I had allowed a gentleman's purse to become an anatomical authority. I told her the purse had purchased precisely the opposite privilege, namely the right to be disappointed later. I did not return the coins. We needed glass more urgently than we needed spotless consciences.
prior_expectations: Patronage would reward refinement
observations: A collector valued the drawing more than its failed subject
decisions: I sold a sketch but refused to sell the specimen
consequences: Money funded new glass while vanity warped the next trial
belief_changes: Praise for appearances was not evidence for vitality
relationship_changes: Mathilde judged the arrangement too close to a theatre ticket
source_anchors: The Lost Years v7 integrated autobiography
alternative_interpretation: Other causes for this recollection remain possible; the narrator is selective.

title: The Cardboard Curtain
memory_text: Henry observed an early growth preparation and immediately began offering improvements to the apparatus. I was pleased for the first ten minutes and exasperated thereafter. He leaned over a vessel during a phase when temperature mattered, and I snatched his sleeve away before he touched the glass. He called my alarm unreasonable. I placed a cardboard screen between the observation table and the doorway and insisted that everyone entering announce himself. Henry said I had turned science into theatre. 'Yes,' I told him, 'and now I shall decide who steps upon the stage.' The screen remained after he departed. It kept drafts from the vessels, which was useful, and curious eyes from my failures, which was more useful than I cared to say. The screen remained when we no longer needed its protection from drafts. I had Lenz paint its outer face black.
prior_expectations: Skilled visitors can inspect developing work without changing it
observations: Henry's proximity threatened temperature-sensitive preparations
decisions: I hung a cardboard screen and required announcing entry
consequences: The screen blocked both air drafts and observation of failure
belief_changes: Experimental control can become control over what witnesses are allowed to see
relationship_changes: Henry resented the performance; I guarded the boundary
alternative_interpretation: The screen's practical draft control was not feigned.

title: Henry's Unsigned Page
memory_text: Henry left a set of drawings beneath my door showing connections between separate organs. The pages contained no signature, though his precise numbering made authorship unmistakable. I corrected a faulty relation and returned them without comment. He confronted me three days later, convinced that silence meant contempt. I told him I had judged the drawing, not its author. He replied that authorship was precisely what frightened him: he feared producing something that would live and therefore belong to neither of us. I laughed at the word 'belong.' He did not. It was one of the first times I saw him hear a moral claim in a problem I considered mechanical. I kept a copy of the diagram and did not tell him so.
prior_expectations: I expected Henry to welcome detached technical criticism
observations: He worried about responsibility and ownership
decisions: I corrected the design and concealed a copy
consequences: A future ethical dispute entered our mentorship
belief_changes: The creator's intentions may not define the created
relationship_changes: Henry trusted my intellect but not my treatment of his fears

title: An Audience of One
memory_text: I prepared a magnificent rebuke to a rival's theory and arranged for Henry to hear it before the lecture. He listened through the first three paragraphs, then asked whether I intended to prove the man wrong or make his supporters uncomfortable. I said that one need not choose. He pointed out a weakness in the fourth paragraph, where my rhetoric exceeded the observed result. I removed the passage and delivered the remainder to a hall so poorly attended that the doorkeeper could count the listeners without moving his lips. Leonie sat at the back repairing a torn glove. Afterward she said the lecture had improved at precisely the point where I stopped pretending an opponent's ignorance was experimental evidence. Henry looked insufferably pleased. I wrote the correction into the blue ledger, then spent most of the evening composing a remark clever enough to convince them that I had conceded nothing. The remark was excellent. Unfortunately they had already gone home.
prior_expectations: A devastating rhetorical performance would establish scientific priority
observations: Henry identified overclaiming and Leonie distinguished demonstration from insult
decisions: I cut the unsupported passage but protected my pride afterward
consequences: My theatricality began to meet resistance from trusted observers
belief_changes: A persuasive attack can be stronger when its unsupported ornament is removed
relationship_changes: Henry acquired the right to contradict me in private, though not without consequences
source_anchors: Source autobiography: 1860-1899, homunculi, dismissal 1868; story added as film-informed fiction
interpretation_basis: Film scholarship suggests critical themes; this event is an invented reconstructed memory

title: A Vessel without a Witness
memory_text: Henry found me watching a minute fleck rise each time I tapped the glass. I called it anticipation. He asked whether it rose when I did not tap. A particularly tiresome question, since no one had proposed holding a séance for a bit of tissue. He folded a card around the side of the vessel, moved the tapping point and found that the fleck no longer rose. He had removed a current I had overlooked. I informed him that invalidating my interpretation did not invalidate the observation, and he agreed, smiling in a way that suggested he had expected a battle. We spent the rest of the afternoon making marks on cork and moving a watch from one end of the bench to the other. When he departed I wrote his suggestion in my ledger. I did not write that he had been pleased to have caught me. That would have made the record unnecessarily human.
prior_expectations: A single observer could recognize genuine advance
observations: Henry found my favored response disappeared when the vessel was rotated
decisions: I repeated the trial in his presence and refused to call the first result fraud
consequences: We began arguing over what counts as independent observation
belief_changes: An unwelcome control may be the only useful result
relationship_changes: Henry acquired permission to challenge my demonstrations
source_anchors: The Lost Years v7 integrated autobiography
alternative_interpretation: Other causes for this recollection remain possible; the narrator is selective.

title: The Unsigned Calculation
memory_text: Henry left a calculation among my papers showing an alternative relationship between the mass of a living preparation and the time required for its recovery. I found an error in the last line, corrected it, and used the amended figure in a private discussion with Heller. Henry overheard enough to believe I had adopted the result without naming him. He was correct. I told him that a student's idea becomes part of his teacher's work when the teacher makes it serviceable. He asked whether the same rule would apply when the student proved the teacher wrong. I had no satisfactory answer ready. That evening I added his initials to the page and left it where he would find it. He never thanked me, and I never repeated the performance. My admiration for his courage did not lessen my appetite for ownership. Both continued to grow.
prior_expectations: I may improve a pupil's work without changing who owns the idea
observations: Henry recognized his uncited calculation in my discussion with Heller
decisions: I restored his initials without offering a public confession
consequences: Henry recovered attribution; my appetite for ownership remained
belief_changes: Respect for a rival and desire to possess his work can coexist
relationship_changes: Henry acquired a concrete grievance and a limited concession
alternative_interpretation: Henry may have expected more public recognition than I understood.

title: The Empty Dish
memory_text: For six weeks I inspected a sealed dish that appeared to contain nothing of interest. Clara advised me to discard it, then changed her mind because I was so eager to agree. Under an oblique light we saw minute structures along one edge, too disordered to call organs and too persistent to call sediment. I fetched Lenz, who pointed out that the dish had been tilted since the previous month. We levelled a second specimen and continued observing both. Neither produced the miracle I anticipated. The first did, however, make its growth follow a path different from that of the second. My ledger acquired an untidy sketch of two branching lines. Later I remembered the sketch more accurately than the specimen.
prior_expectations: I expected a blank vessel to contain no development
observations: Two environmental positions correlated with different growth patterns
decisions: I kept comparative dishes under observation
consequences: Evidence accumulated without a life-creation claim
belief_changes: Growth conditions can bias form
relationship_changes: Clara and Lenz constrained my tendency to announce success

title: The Drawing Returned
memory_text: Theodor received an offer to prepare architectural drawings in another city. I met him at Leonie's workroom, where half-completed costumes hung like people unwilling to commit themselves to a profession. He showed me the terms of employment. They were good, although not so good that I could not find objections. He asked whether I wished him to decline. The room contained an empty chair and a bowl of pins. I considered telling him that the laboratory would soon produce results worth witnessing. Instead I explained that advancement ought not to be sacrificed to an arrangement whose terms neither of us had properly established. He repeated the word arrangement as though testing a badly made hinge. He returned my lens wrapped in the theatre drawing on which we had first disagreed. I congratulated him on his future and left before Leonie could introduce sympathy into the discussion. Three months later I discovered that I had been consulting his notes on perspective while marking an anatomical proof. His absence had become useful to me as an excuse for a number of errors which were wholly mine.
prior_expectations: A good employment offer would settle the decision painlessly
observations: Theodor asked whether I wanted him to remain
decisions: I praised his advancement instead of asking him to stay
consequences: A valued intimate partnership receded into correspondence
belief_changes: Defending autonomy could conceal fear of asking for care
relationship_changes: Theodor left with affection unresolved and trust reduced
source_anchors: Original autobiography: pre-reunion chronology and boundary, fictional authority
v6 baseline: preserved surrounding scenes and relationships
New adult interpersonal incident: reconstructed fiction, no original source citation
alternative_interpretation: Separation may have served both men's ambitions without coercion

title: The Little Arm That Wasn't
memory_text: For eleven days I drew a splendid little arm, bent at the elbow, terminating in what might almost have been a hand. I drew it from the same place at the same hour, with the lamp to my left. Lenz arrived carrying a repaired stopper and, without consulting my scientific dignity, lifted the vessel onto a felt pad. The arm vanished. He rotated it once more and showed me an innocent membrane, folded by a distortion in his own curved glass. I called the workmanship criminal. He asked whether I should prefer the glassblower to have manufactured the limb itself. The replacement vessel had one flat wall, an atrocity to look upon and a great improvement to the eye. I kept the old sketches. When I saw the handsome false arm again, I remembered not how I had been deceived but how very quickly I had wished to be.
prior_expectations: An elegant contour signified differentiation
observations: The supposed limb was a fold seen through curved glass
decisions: I paid Lenz to remake the vessel with an inelegant flat wall
consequences: Weeks of confident sketches became a warning against optics
belief_changes: I grew suspicious of perfect outlines under perfect light
relationship_changes: Lenz gained unusual freedom to criticize my apparatus
source_anchors: The Lost Years v7 integrated autobiography
alternative_interpretation: Other causes for this recollection remain possible; the narrator is selective.

title: A Door Measured Twice
memory_text: Kappel warned me that a committee member had begun asking about deliveries to the private rooms. I accused him of enjoying the role of sentry. Clara had heard a second rumor from a supplier, one concerning not the apparatus but the safety of our sealed vessels. I measured the room doors, arranged for a second lock, and composed a statement about harmless botanical investigation. It was accurate as far as it went and designed to make further questions appear unnecessary. When Kappel saw the statement he said I had managed to write the truth so that nobody could find it. I admired the description enough to repeat it later as a joke. The lock deterred visitors and delayed Lenz one cold morning while a vessel overheated. We installed an emergency latch. Secrecy had protected my work and endangered it within the same fortnight. I kept the lock.
prior_expectations: Privacy of a scientific room is an unqualified safeguard
observations: A guarded doorway also made emergency access difficult
decisions: I measured the door and installed an additional escape latch
consequences: The laboratory became simultaneously more secret and more accessible in emergencies
belief_changes: Sovereignty imposes design costs that rhetoric cannot erase
relationship_changes: Kappel and Clara pressed practical constraints on my secrecy
alternative_interpretation: A simple building defect, not secrecy, could account for the danger.

title: The Winter Inventory
memory_text: At year's end we took stock. Lenz's figures showed how much I owed him, Clara's which samples had lost their labels, mine the discouraging number of failures that I preferred to call incomplete trials. We agreed no undated vessel could constitute evidence. It was a good rule, and I disliked its immediate application to three preparations in which I had invested considerable hope. The next morning Lenz's wife left bread, cheese, and a note instructing me to eat before extinguishing the second lamp. I ate the bread standing at my bench. The cheese was excellent, the note intolerably familiar. I kept the note under a weight for weeks, ostensibly because it was the only clean scrap of paper within reach.
prior_expectations: I expected the year's work to justify its expense
observations: We found significant identification and accounting failures
decisions: I accepted strict labelling and rationed materials
consequences: Research slowed but became traceable
belief_changes: Survival of a specimen is not evidence without history
relationship_changes: Lenz's household entered my life as a source of unasked practical care

title: The Vessel That Would Not Answer
memory_text: A preparation gave no coherent response for nineteen successive observations. I had begun speaking of it to Lenz as though the vessel were deliberately withholding consent. Clara asked whether the heating schedule had changed. I replied that the schedule had not changed and produced my ledger as proof. She pointed out that I had recorded intended temperatures rather than those taken at the glass. We measured again and found a difference sufficient to ruin my interpretation. I scraped my proposed account from the slate and ordered another week of observations. The preparation's behavior altered after the correction, though I could not prove that the correction alone caused it. I remember Clara's forefinger on the wrong column of the ledger. I purchased a second thermometer for Clara to read and was disagreeably attentive whenever its figures differed from mine.
prior_expectations: A failed vessel proves either its preparation or its maker incompetent
observations: Clara detected a procedural assumption within nineteen negative observations
decisions: I repeated controls under her proposed conditions
consequences: The results became more interpretable without producing instant triumph
belief_changes: Error may lie in my account of the test, not in the specimen
relationship_changes: Clara gained access to the logic of my experiments, not merely supplies
alternative_interpretation: The altered result may remain contingent on uncontrolled conditions.

title: The Dullest Sunday
memory_text: I had been in the laboratory since Saturday, troubling a stubborn vessel with inspections that produced nothing but a sore neck. At nine the church bells began. I was tempted to declare the entire culture dead and salvage my Sunday by declaring an enemy defeated. Clara called to fetch me for an inventory of ordinary medicines. I followed her because the lamp oil had run out and because she offered coffee without discussing my theories. We counted bottles, argued about a missing label, and ate hard bread with cheese. When I returned at dusk the vessel was precisely as it had been. I was absurdly gratified by this evidence that the world could continue to resist me without requiring my constant supervision. On Monday it moved. I would have preferred it to do so while I was watching, naturally.
prior_expectations: Relentless attention would accelerate development
observations: The most promising material showed no new activity despite constant handling
decisions: I left it undisturbed and spent the morning with Clara's inventory
consequences: Progress followed no timetable I could command
belief_changes: Interference could be a form of impatience rather than care
relationship_changes: Clara saw me capable of leaving a specimen alone briefly
source_anchors: The Lost Years v7 integrated autobiography
alternative_interpretation: Other causes for this recollection remain possible; the narrator is selective.

title: The First Coherent Response
memory_text: I shall not describe the preparation of the seed. The formula is not relevant to the recollection and I have no intention of donating it to posterity. What matters is that one minute developing form turned toward an intermittent shadow and continued to orient itself after the shadow was removed. Lenz suggested a mechanical response to heat. Clara changed the light and asked us to try again. We did. The little form did not behave like the first series of samples. I remained at the bench until my knees trembled, then went out to buy more candles. The grocer asked whether I had been drinking. I had not, which made the question particularly irritating. I wrote 'possible organized response' in the blue ledger and underlined 'possible.'
prior_expectations: I expected only passive tissue reaction
observations: A developing form displayed repeatable orientation under altered conditions
decisions: I recorded restrained observations and requested replication
consequences: The first candidate for autonomous miniature life emerged
belief_changes: Coordinated response was possible but not yet proof of consciousness
relationship_changes: Clara trusted the measurement more than my interpretation; Lenz questioned heat artifacts

title: A Queen Without a Court
memory_text: After the first coherent response and before I had cultivated the others, the Queen occupied a small platform alone. I placed two objects where she could choose between them, intending to test a preference for height. She moved neither. She stood at the far edge with her back to me while I made increasingly persuasive adjustments. Lenz suggested that my arrangement resembled a trap. I laughed, then moved my hands from the vessel and waited. She crossed to the lower object when she was no longer under my shadow. I wrote 'avoidance of overhead obstruction.' Clara wrote 'possibly of you' in the margin. The distinction was not resolved. I have always enjoyed exercising command. My first sovereign subject made the enjoyment more interesting by failing to obey, and I grew absurdly eager to understand the terms of her refusal.
prior_expectations: A newly created sovereign should acknowledge the hand that made her
observations: The Queen responded to changing light and withheld the greeting I expected
decisions: I varied observation conditions rather than abandon the title
consequences: I became invested in her resistant routines
belief_changes: My creation's behavior could become an object of rivalry with my intentions
relationship_changes: Clara challenged my anthropomorphic account without destroying my fascination
alternative_interpretation: A response to light need not be defiance.

title: A Face Too Complete
memory_text: The little figure now possessed the beginnings of a face. One side was finer than the other, and I wasted a morning attempting to view the discrepancy as a trick of reflected light. Henry considered its response to an approaching shadow more important than the uneven jaw. Clara asked whether I intended to accuse it of bad breeding. I found both remarks provincial. Nevertheless I abandoned the drawing with its invented symmetry and sat beside the vessel until the shadows lengthened. When I approached with a silver mirror the creature turned away from the brightest patch. If it could choose its comfort over my preferred view, it had advanced beyond any portrait I might devise. I did not describe the episode in these sentimental terms to Henry. I merely forbade him to touch the lamp.
prior_expectations: The first responsive figure should be perfected before presentation
observations: The developing features were uneven though responses remained coherent
decisions: I withheld the drawing and continued watching rather than correcting the asymmetry
consequences: My impatience gave way to a reluctant interval of observation
belief_changes: A living expression could exceed its measured proportions
relationship_changes: Henry attended with care; Clara disliked my word defect
source_anchors: The Lost Years v7 integrated autobiography
alternative_interpretation: Other causes for this recollection remain possible; the narrator is selective.

title: Her Majesty's Refusal
memory_text: The Queen was the first. I named her days after she had begun to live, when it became clear she had no intention of behaving like a laboratory ornament. She favored one ledge and returned to it after every change of arrangement. I rotated the vessel; Clara argued that light would explain the preference. The little sovereign ascended the ledge once more, surveyed my enormous face, and withdrew to an entirely different corner. I said she had made her choice, a scientific description to which Clara objected. Perhaps the creature only wanted shade. It is difficult to be certain when one's kingdom is made of glass and one's creator is forever breathing upon it. I spent that night in a chair beside her and woke with an excellent idea and a thoroughly ruined neck.
prior_expectations: I expected the successful creature to obey imposed arrangements
observations: The Queen repeatedly chose and then abandoned a favored ledge
decisions: I observed rather than force her location
consequences: The first homunculus gained an enduring identity in my notes
belief_changes: Created life may have preferences separate from my design
relationship_changes: Clara resisted anthropomorphic certainty; I began a possessive attachment to the Queen

title: The Borrowed Royal Title
memory_text: Henry asked why I called the first creature a Queen when she possessed no subjects. I answered that royalty preceded its court in numerous European histories. Clara suggested that I wanted her disobedience to look ceremonial. Henry smiled too readily. To settle the matter I placed a small paper throne in the vessel and watched the Queen disassemble one arm of it. I was delighted, an inconvenient admission since my hypothesis had been insulted in miniature. Henry took the broken arm home to sketch its joinery and returned it with a note about leverage. I kept the note and not the throne. A name can be an observation, a hope, or a demand imposed upon something that has not agreed to bear it. I persisted in calling her Majesty. She continued to behave as if the title conferred no obligation whatever.
prior_expectations: A title bestowed by a creator creates a relationship of obligation
observations: Henry questioned what the Queen's rank could mean without a court
decisions: I kept the name while refining experiments around her activity
consequences: I began distinguishing my imposed significance from her observed preference
belief_changes: Naming can express the author's desire rather than the subject's state
relationship_changes: Henry exposed the possessiveness within my terminology
alternative_interpretation: Royal naming may simply be aesthetic play.

title: The Queen and the Velvet
memory_text: When Leonie first saw the Queen she did not exclaim over the miracle. She asked why the platform was draped in velvet when the creature repeatedly sought the uncovered edge. I explained that velvet lent dignity and protected her from reflected glare. Leonie placed a narrow strip of plain linen beside the purple fold and withdrew her hand. The Queen approached the linen and sat with her back to my arrangement. Clara advised us to repeat the observation under different light. We did so. The result was irritatingly consistent. Leonie removed the velvet and asked what dignity was worth to a being who could neither purchase it nor consent to its price. I answered that beauty mattered even when its intended audience was ungrateful. The Queen then tugged a thread free and examined it more attentively than she had ever examined me. I recorded that the linen had displaced an aesthetic preference. I did not specify whose preference. Leonie noticed, but did not insist on a correction.
prior_expectations: The Queen would respond favorably to a more splendid setting
observations: She repeatedly chose a plain textile over the velvet I preferred
decisions: I retained the result while obscuring the ownership of the preference
consequences: My aesthetic conception encountered an independent living preference
belief_changes: Creation does not ensure that beauty will be perceived as the creator expects
relationship_changes: Leonie became a witness to my selective reporting
source_anchors: Source autobiography: 1860-1899, homunculi, dismissal 1868; story added as film-informed fiction
interpretation_basis: Film scholarship suggests critical themes; this event is an invented reconstructed memory

title: Velvet Does Not Make a Sovereign
memory_text: Leonie brought a remnant of violet velvet from a theatre costume. I cut a seat for the Queen and had it fitted beneath her favored ledge. The little monarch approached, placed one hand upon the cloth and retreated with unmistakable dispatch. I blamed the dye. Clara blamed my conceit. Leonie, who had pinned costumes onto living performers for years, suggested that the nap scratched. I touched it with my finger and felt nothing. She put the smallest splinter of thread against the sensitive skin of my wrist. I felt it perfectly then. We replaced the velvet with a plain strip of polished wood and the Queen returned. I kept the scrap in an envelope labelled REGALIA REJECTED. It amused me to imagine a monarch whose taste could not be bought, even with fabric of a most expensive shade.
prior_expectations: A throne would elicit more regal conduct
observations: The Queen preferred an undecorated ledge and avoided the theatrical velvet
decisions: I removed the cloth but kept a tiny embroidered scrap
consequences: I learned decoration could be offensive to its intended subject
belief_changes: Taste could belong to the creation rather than to the creator
relationship_changes: Leonie stopped treating my arrangements as neutral science
source_anchors: The Lost Years v7 integrated autobiography
alternative_interpretation: Other causes for this recollection remain possible; the narrator is selective.

title: A King with an Inconvenient Heart
memory_text: The second creature emerged with the complacent features of Henry VIII, a resemblance which I confess gave me disproportionate delight. He fastened his attention on the Queen and neglected his food when her vessel was removed. I called it attachment. Clara called it distress. Neither of us possessed an instrument capable of settling the matter, but I had one capable of ending the knocking against the glass: I restored the Queen to his sight. He ate. There was a vulgar triumph in being obeyed by a king, although I did not then appreciate which party had issued the command. I separated their vessels less often afterward. A mere convenience, I told visitors, as though I had not rearranged half the bench to accommodate a creature smaller than my thumb.
prior_expectations: I expected a second creation to behave as a separate specimen
observations: The King repeatedly oriented toward the Queen and neglected feeding
decisions: I changed placement and began recording proximity effects
consequences: Their relationship constrained daily practice
belief_changes: Social dependence may emerge without instruction
relationship_changes: The King became an object of affectionate irritation; Clara became an advocate of welfare

title: The Seat Beside the King
memory_text: Henry spent a disagreeable afternoon measuring the distance the King travelled toward the Queen when her jar was brought near. He proposed that attraction might be a response to movement or warmth. I suggested that the King possessed a taste for the unattainable, which made him the least original monarch in history. Leonie had been asked to sew a curtain for the testing alcove. She watched us move the jars about as though arranging a marriage between porcelain figures, then asked what evidence would persuade us that the King wished for something else. Henry answered at once. I offered a more elaborate answer and took longer. We repeated the trial with an empty jar and discovered, to my amusement, that the King approached the motion even without his sovereign. The result did not extinguish my romantic explanation. It merely made it less sufficient. I preserved both in the ledger, one in ink and one in the margin, where a candid man might have reversed their positions.
prior_expectations: The King's pursuit of the Queen expressed stable personal attachment
observations: Moving an empty jar also attracted his attention
decisions: I logged the instrumental result and my preferred interpretation
consequences: My sentimental reading survived a counterexample but lost certainty
belief_changes: An attractive narrative may outlive the observation that challenged it
relationship_changes: Henry's analytic caution became more valuable and more annoying
source_anchors: Source autobiography: 1860-1899, homunculi, dismissal 1868; story added as film-informed fiction
interpretation_basis: Film scholarship suggests critical themes; this event is an invented reconstructed memory

title: The King's Nose
memory_text: I compared the King's face with an engraving of Henry VIII, then with a wax bust borrowed from a collector whose trust in my scholarship deserved a better fate. From the left, the resemblance was delicious. From the right, he might have been a provincial tax official with a very small grievance. Henry said I had chosen the Tudor king because my miniature already disapproved of being contradicted. Lenz proposed that we rotate the engraving until history behaved. I laughed more than the joke warranted, then measured the profile again. The numbers refused my preferred comparison. In the ledger I wrote that the resemblance was evocative, not diagnostic. At dinner I told the story as though the King himself had selected the model. Scholars must sometimes be permitted a little poetic licence after correcting their own diagrams.
prior_expectations: Historical resemblance would prove aesthetic intention
observations: The King did not resemble the bust from every angle
decisions: I retained the nickname while rejecting the measurement
consequences: The resemblance became a joke and an object of public myth
belief_changes: A witty analogy should not be mistaken for a biological finding
relationship_changes: Henry teased my historical comparisons; Lenz enjoyed them
source_anchors: The Lost Years v7 integrated autobiography
alternative_interpretation: Other causes for this recollection remain possible; the narrator is selective.

title: The Archbishop's Objection
memory_text: A third little figure developed in an attitude of disapproval so sustained that we named him Archbishop before his clothing had properly formed. He interrupted the King's displays by striking a tiny staff against the base of his vessel. Lenz, who found this uproariously funny, positioned the jars so that the King could see both the Queen and the Archbishop. The result was a three-sided quarrel conducted with gestures too small to hear. I intended to study hierarchy and instead spent the morning shifting glass to prevent injury. Clara pointed out that the Archbishop did not object to the Queen at all, only to the King approaching her. I had assigned a theological motive to an observation that did not require one. The distinction displeased me because it was interesting.
prior_expectations: I expected an ecclesiastical-looking form to signal doctrinal opposition
observations: The Archbishop objected specifically to the King's proximity
decisions: I rearranged jars to prevent collision
consequences: Social interactions altered the apparatus
belief_changes: Names can distort interpretation of behavior
relationship_changes: I began to credit Clara's alternative reading of the Archbishop

title: A Pamphlet Read Twice
memory_text: I read one of Karl Heinrich Ulrichs's tracts in a Munich printer's waiting room in 1867. Its arguments about men whose affections turned toward men were expressed with a lawyer's appetite for categories, several of which I found biologically unpersuasive. Yet the candor of the enterprise was remarkable. He did not petition for a toleration disguised as illness; he demanded that the law explain its own jurisdiction. I made notes in the margin, then tore them out because I had written upon a borrowed copy. A printer's assistant asked whether I knew the author's work. I said that I knew an argument when I saw one, regardless of its author's domestic arrangements. It was a clever answer and a cowardly one, a combination in which I had lately become proficient. I bought another copy before leaving. I did not meet Ulrichs and have no right to borrow his courage for my own account. His printed words did, however, make a question I had considered private appear on a public page.
prior_expectations: Private feeling had no serious place in printed legal argument
observations: Ulrichs argued publicly for men with same-sex desire
decisions: I read and bought the pamphlet without claiming kinship
consequences: A private question became an articulated public controversy
belief_changes: The ethics of classification and civic standing could be discussed
relationship_changes: A deadening distinction between public courage and personal avoidance appeared
source_anchors: Original autobiography: pre-reunion chronology and boundary, fictional authority
v6 baseline: preserved surrounding scenes and relationships
New adult interpersonal incident: reconstructed fiction, no original source citation
Historical: Ulrichs published pamphlets beginning in 1864 and publicly advocated in Munich in 1867, https://forummuenchen.org/projekte/steckbriefe-zu-lgbtiq-persoenlichkeiten/karl-heinrich-ulrichs/
alternative_interpretation: Intellectual agreement did not require adopting Ulrichs's categories

title: The Servant Who Saw Too Much
memory_text: A porter found a broken crate bearing the markings of Lenz's workshop and asked what sort of glass required so much straw and such nervous instructions. Kappel told him it was fragile research material. The porter asked whether fragile research material ordinarily seemed to be knocking at its own box. The sound was a loose wooden cleat, as we discovered when the crate was opened; the story had already acquired a heartbeat by the time it reached the porter's friends. I was furious that a stupid accident should be more persuasive than three years of careful work. Kappel proposed admitting a neutral observer to dispel suspicion. I refused. Each alternative offended me differently: secrecy encouraged legend, publicity endangered control. I chose control. When the story reached the faculty corridor, the crate had acquired a second knock and a small creature that I had never grown.
prior_expectations: A trustworthy servant will treat laboratory deliveries as unremarkable
observations: A porter saw a damaged crate and reported unfamiliar glassware
decisions: I arranged more concealed transport and stricter access
consequences: Secrecy reduced casual witnesses but increased suspicion
belief_changes: Information control can manufacture the hostility it anticipates
relationship_changes: Kappel aided precautions but remained concerned about the consequences
alternative_interpretation: The porter may have been merely curious rather than suspicious.

title: The Archbishop's Unanswered Prayer
memory_text: I set a minute altar near the Archbishop's chamber, an exquisite piece of folded paper, and rang a silver bell while he stood before it. He did not bow. He did not cross himself. He went very still when the bell sounded, and afterward moved toward the place from which the vibration came. I said he was attending to a summons. Clara asked whose summons, God's or mine. I told her those were not invariably distinct in a laboratory. She declined to laugh. We altered the interval of the sound and moved the altar, which remained of no interest whatever. I entered his response under SOUND, not DEVOTION. The little altar stayed on a shelf for months. Its uselessness offended me, because the folds were more elegant than the majority of churches I knew.
prior_expectations: Symbolic objects might elicit familiar ceremonial conduct
observations: The Archbishop responded consistently to the bell but ignored the little altar
decisions: I removed the altar and varied the bell's timing
consequences: The distinction between response and interpretation grew harder to ignore
belief_changes: Religious titles were mine, sensory preferences might be his
relationship_changes: Clara insisted I record what happened before interpreting it
source_anchors: The Lost Years v7 integrated autobiography
alternative_interpretation: Other causes for this recollection remain possible; the narrator is selective.

title: The Man in the Black Cape
memory_text: I had not intended to cultivate anything resembling myself. Nonetheless the fourth figure emerged lean, dark and rather theatrical, with a black cape whose folds appeared before the rest of his costume had assumed proper definition. Lenz called him the Devil. Henry, shown the figure during one carefully supervised visit, regarded him with more unease than he had shown at the Queen. The Devil bowed toward his reflection in the glass and then turned his back upon us. I was delighted. Henry asked whether the miniature had learned vanity from its maker. I told him that resemblance proved kinship no more reliably than a portrait proved paternity. Yet I moved the little mirror out of the laboratory afterward. Certain jokes are more uncomfortable when they resemble observations.
prior_expectations: I expected morphology to be controllable and distinct from my own image
observations: A dark-caped homunculus performed before a reflection
decisions: I recorded the behavior and removed the mirror
consequences: Henry witnessed a creation but remained unsettled
belief_changes: Apparent imitation need not prove inherited intention
relationship_changes: Henry's admiration mixed with alarm; Lenz teased me more freely

title: The Second Set of Figures
memory_text: I prepared one table for scientific use and another for a prospective patron, removing the damaged observations from the second because they would require more explanation than the fellow could bear. Henry discovered the discrepancy and asked whether a result made prettier for money remained a result. I replied that I had omitted noise, not evidence. He laid the two sheets side by side and pointed to a small irregularity that appeared in three of the supposedly noisy readings. Clara examined it, then asked for the original notebooks. We reinstated the figures. The patron saw both versions and declined to support us. I cursed Henry's delicacy and Clara's stubbornness. A fortnight later the irregularity helped us detect a recurrent fault in the apparatus. I sent Henry a copy of the revised table without comment. He wrote 'I see it' on the back. I have retained that scrap longer than the patron's name.
prior_expectations: A public-facing result may properly omit untidy failures
observations: Henry noticed I had prepared a selectively flattering account for a patron
decisions: I retained fuller figures and ultimately abandoned the misleading table
consequences: The scrap marked by Henry outlasted the prospective patron
belief_changes: Credit and evidence become unstable when display outruns observation
relationship_changes: Henry found an opening to question my private standards
alternative_interpretation: I may have cared as much about Henry's judgment as about the data.

title: The Crown Nobody Asked For
locations: Leonie's workroom and private laboratory, Ingolstadt
memory_text: Leonie produced a crown small enough for the Queen, using fine wire and a red glass bead Lenz had rejected as imperfect. It was beautifully made. I rewarded the gift with an inventory of its historical errors, then carried it to the laboratory in a cotton-lined box. The Queen stood beneath it for several moments without attempting to take it. When I opened the cabinet the following morning, the crown lay behind a feeding dish. I accused Lenz of having brushed it aside. He showed me where the Queen had dragged it herself, leaving a trail in the damp medium. Leonie laughed when I told her. She asked whether the Queen was a more discerning patron than I. I said she had the same intolerable inclination to judge a gift by whether she wanted it. Nevertheless, before returning the crown to its box I repaired the bent wire myself. I took uncommon care with a thing its intended owner appeared to dislike.
prior_expectations: The Queen would accept the crown as an expression of rank
observations: She displaced it without ceremony
decisions: I preserved and repaired the unwanted object
consequences: Gifts came to register the maker's attachment more than the recipient's preference
belief_changes: The creator's sentiment need not be reciprocated
relationship_changes: Leonie's gift acquired private significance despite my criticism
source_anchors: Source autobiography: 1860-1899, homunculi, dismissal 1868; story added as film-informed fiction
interpretation_basis: Film scholarship suggests critical themes; this event is an invented reconstructed memory

title: The Devil's Reflection
memory_text: The Devil came to his little cape by means of Leonie's sewing, not infernal providence. She insisted that the shoulders must fall correctly if the garment was to be seen through glass. I held a polished spoon beside my own face and challenged Henry to name the likeness. He said the creature seemed less inclined than I to interrupt a companion. I found this unscientific, and may have been less gracious about the observation than my confidence deserved. The little gentleman paused before his reflection, examined it and walked away. Leonie suggested he had better things to do than admire his own face. I put the spoon in a drawer and explained that its curvature rendered it useless as an instrument. I used it thereafter to stir my gin, where inaccuracies of proportion were rather welcome.
prior_expectations: The Devil's resemblance to me would be obvious
observations: Visitors disagreed over which features constituted the likeness
decisions: I permitted the cape but refused to label the face
consequences: The creature became a private joke that sometimes irritated me
belief_changes: Vanity is easiest disguised as a comparative study
relationship_changes: Leonie saw more of my amusement than Henry did
source_anchors: The Lost Years v7 integrated autobiography
alternative_interpretation: Other causes for this recollection remain possible; the narrator is selective.

title: Music Before Supper
memory_text: The Ballerina responded to Mendelssohn's 'Spring Song' and to very little else we tried. Clara first played the phrase on an ill-tuned piano in the room below, and the tiny dancer rose from her resting place. When the tune stopped, so did she. I assumed any melody in the same tempo would serve; she refused three substitutions, one played so badly that I sympathized with her judgment. A week later Clara was delayed, and I found myself humming at the jar while stirring soup. The Ballerina did not move. I ate the soup cold and waited for Clara's return. This dependence on a particular piece of music made the laboratory less controllable, and, to my surprise, considerably more pleasant.
prior_expectations: I expected general rhythmic stimulation to elicit dance
observations: Only a specific Mendelssohn piece consistently preceded movement
decisions: I preserved that musical cue instead of imposing alternatives
consequences: The Ballerina acquired a daily ritual
belief_changes: Preference can be highly specific rather than a generic reflex
relationship_changes: Clara became the favored musician; I accepted a small daily inconvenience

title: The Room Before the Committee
memory_text: When word came that the faculty might ask to inspect the laboratory, I spent an evening placing the vessels in a configuration that would compel attention. The Queen stood at the center, the Archbishop to one side and the King opposite, as though judgment and appetite were offices of state. Leonie arrived to repair a curtain and said the arrangement made the little people resemble evidence staged for a trial whose outcome I had already decided. Kappel recommended that I place the ordinary observation books at the front. I refused because their inconsistent figures would distract from the central achievement. Leonie pushed a lamp two inches left and transformed the composition so completely that I allowed her to finish. Then, when both visitors had gone, I put the irregular books beneath the table. I have never found it difficult to tell when others are concealing facts. With myself, naturally, the distinction between selection and concealment requires a finer instrument.
prior_expectations: The spectacle would persuade any fair examiner
observations: Trusted advisers noticed that the display concealed inconvenient measurements
decisions: I staged the vessels and hid inconsistent notebooks
consequences: Public display and scientific record became dangerously separable
belief_changes: Control of a presentation can also control what observers are allowed to know
relationship_changes: Kappel and Leonie resisted my instinct to curate evidence
source_anchors: Source autobiography: 1860-1899, homunculi, dismissal 1868; story added as film-informed fiction
interpretation_basis: Film scholarship suggests critical themes; this event is an invented reconstructed memory

title: The Ballerina Refuses an Encore
memory_text: I had arranged for the Ballerina's favored music to be played three times to impress a private guest. She danced through the first rendition, paused before the conclusion of the second, and refused altogether to respond to the third. I blamed the pianist, who was not present. Leonie played the melody softly once more after an hour of silence, and the tiny dancer raised one arm before sitting down. Leonie asked what would happen to a human dancer obliged to repeat the same figure without rest until an audience was persuaded of its existence. I said we were discussing a creation, not a theatre contract. Yet I sent my guest away and shortened the subsequent sessions. I still liked an encore. I found I liked it better when it was offered rather than exacted.
prior_expectations: Repetition of the favored melody guaranteed repeated movement
observations: The Ballerina stopped at a familiar passage and resumed only after quiet
decisions: I dismissed the small audience and shortened the session
consequences: Performance ceased to be a reliable synonym for health
belief_changes: A preference may include a preference to stop
relationship_changes: Leonie protested that I had turned music into a command
source_anchors: The Lost Years v7 integrated autobiography
alternative_interpretation: Other causes for this recollection remain possible; the narrator is selective.

title: Salt in the Water
memory_text: The seaweed arrived leaking brine through three layers of paper and a courier's protest. From it, by means I shall not publish, came the Mermaid. She occupied her watery chamber in such perfect stillness that I feared a beautiful failure. Clara discovered that she moved when visitors departed. We watched from behind a screen, uncomfortably bent like burglars in our own laboratory, while the little figure rose and vanished among the weed. I wrote 'timid' in the ledger. Later I drew a line through it and added 'reacts to observers.' I have not destroyed the first word. It remains possible that she was timid, and equally possible that she possessed an excellent opinion of the advantages of avoiding me.
prior_expectations: I expected the aquatic specimen to display activity for observers
observations: The Mermaid moved more freely without an audience
decisions: I built a screened observation routine
consequences: A sixth distinctive homunculus survived
belief_changes: Nonperformance is not evidence of incapacity
relationship_changes: Clara defended the Mermaid against my impatient interpretation

title: The Private Invitation
memory_text: Heller came privately rather than sending for me. He had heard descriptions of the miniature beings and wished to see evidence before the faculty was obliged to act upon rumor. Henry urged me to admit him. Clara said the conditions could be arranged if Heller agreed to observe without disturbing the vessels. I prepared three drafts of an invitation. Each seemed to surrender something to a man who might afterwards vote upon my work. In the end I showed Heller selected records and declined to open the inner room. He examined the curves and asked whether the living forms could choose not to be examined. I called this a moral question smuggled into a technical visit. He said technical questions frequently acquire occupants. We parted without an agreement. I still wonder whether a demonstration would have altered his conduct. That is not the same as wishing I had given him one.
prior_expectations: Heller should either accept my work on my conditions or remain excluded
observations: Heller offered a private viewing under terms I distrusted
decisions: I refused a demonstration and preserved the locked method
consequences: I lost a possible advocate without learning what he might have said
belief_changes: A refusal protects sovereignty while foreclosing potentially useful evidence
relationship_changes: My relationship with Heller acquired a permanently undecidable counterfactual
alternative_interpretation: Heller's proposal may have been an honest attempt at support.

title: The Cabinet of Flawless Things
memory_text: Reuter found a drawer lined in blue felt. It contained the things I had spared the wastebasket because they were handsome: a transparent shell, a minute symmetrical form that had never responded, and a delicate branching structure that suggested intelligence only if one wished it. He asked where I had put their dates and controls. I was furious at the implication that beauty had no probative force. Then I discovered I could not remember which of two nearly identical specimens had been kept warm. I took my pen and labelled the drawer AESTHETIC, NOT EVIDENCE, before he could do it for me. He looked disappointed rather than triumphant. We closed the drawer. It remains the only collection in my laboratory for which I refuse to manufacture a scientific justification.
prior_expectations: Preserving handsome failures would explain my developmental method
observations: Reuter found my best-preserved specimens lacked usable experimental records
decisions: I marked the drawer AESTHETIC, NOT EVIDENCE
consequences: A secret display acquired its own rules
belief_changes: Collecting evidence and collecting beauty are different occupations
relationship_changes: Reuter became less willing to accept my demonstrations without books
source_anchors: The Lost Years v7 integrated autobiography
alternative_interpretation: Other causes for this recollection remain possible; the narrator is selective.

title: The Visit from the Committee
locations: University of Ingolstadt, faculty committee room
memory_text: The committee arrived with the solemnity of undertakers pricing a living man. Its charges were conduct unbecoming my office and experiments injurious to the moral fabric of the university, a textile evidently too delicate to survive a six-inch vessel. I offered observations and withheld my method. Heller read the pages while two others inspected my face as if the proof of corruption might be found there. A younger member asked if the little beings suffered. I spoke on the difficulty of defining suffering, with all the authority I could assemble. The question remained unanswered. Henry waited outside and said afterward that my discourse had done us no good. I reminded him that a good answer and a useful answer are not necessarily the same. He looked less comforted than I had intended.
prior_expectations: I expected documented success to win intellectual legitimacy
observations: The committee asked ethical questions I deflected and demanded a complete method
decisions: I submitted observations but withheld the formula
consequences: The disciplinary inquiry intensified
belief_changes: Empirical success does not settle obligations toward created beings
relationship_changes: Henry's loyalty became strained; Heller separated doubt from condemnation

title: The Joke in the Corridor
memory_text: Heller passed me outside the committee room without returning my greeting. Several junior scholars stood nearby pretending to examine a noticeboard. I said, distinctly enough for all to hear, that the faculty had at last discovered a form of life it could create without my assistance: the administrative parasite. Someone laughed, too quickly and then not at all. Leonie had come to retrieve a garment from my rooms and overheard the exchange. She told me afterward that the joke was clever and had cost me the last possibility of a sympathetic hearing. I answered that a sympathetic hearing obtained through silence was merely a conviction postponed. She said there were times when preserving one's options was not cowardice. I began a reply, decided it would require more than the corridor deserved, and went upstairs to pack the samples. The same young scholar who laughed later refused to meet my eyes. I remember his embarrassment more sharply than Heller's silence.
prior_expectations: Public mockery would restore dignity in a humiliating institutional setting
observations: The joke impressed bystanders but worsened my position
decisions: I chose a memorable insult over tactical restraint
consequences: Wit became a costly reflex in conflicts with power
belief_changes: Verbal mastery does not translate into institutional leverage
relationship_changes: Leonie's judgment remained unwelcome but credible
source_anchors: Source autobiography: 1860-1899, homunculi, dismissal 1868; story added as film-informed fiction
interpretation_basis: Film scholarship suggests critical themes; this event is an invented reconstructed memory

title: The List I Did Not Submit
memory_text: While the faculty prepared its questions I made an inventory of every instrument, culture, invoice and living vessel in my care. It grew into an indictment of the institution, including the names of men and women whose labor had permitted my work. Lenz delivered a broken clamp and warned that an inquiry could travel along a receipt as easily as an accusation. Clara said that my witnesses had not all volunteered to become defendants. I drew a line through several suppliers and removed the pages concerning arrangements never approved by any committee. Whether this was loyalty, vanity or simple prudence depends upon who tells the story. I placed the full inventory in a sealed envelope. My shorter reply did not save my chair. It did not condemn everyone who had sat near it either.
prior_expectations: An inventory would silence the faculty
observations: The same list might expose assistants and confidential suppliers
decisions: I submitted an abbreviated list with crucial procedures withheld
consequences: The hearing remained partly opaque even to later correspondents
belief_changes: Public vindication was not worth every private name
relationship_changes: Clara understood the omission but questioned my motives
source_anchors: The Lost Years v7 integrated autobiography
alternative_interpretation: Other causes for this recollection remain possible; the narrator is selective.

title: A Request for Reconsideration
memory_text: The committee had heard its witnesses by June, though it had not yet pronounced sentence. I was allowed to submit a statement of reconsideration. Kappel brought me the official form, two pages of ruled paper, and advice to say that the observations were incomplete and the circumstances regrettable. I wrote that they were incomplete because life itself was not finished and that regret would not improve a measurement. Heller, who had come to collect another document, read the page with a tired expression. He said that I had once been capable of winning an argument without forcing an enemy to lose his dignity. I asked whether the committee had extended me that courtesy. He did not answer. I filed the statement. For many years I told the story as one of heroic refusal. Sometimes I remember the unused sheet Kappel had left beneath my hand, and that I might have written something else without falsifying a single fact.
prior_expectations: A public defense of truth should require no concessions of manner
observations: The committee offered reconsideration while pressing me to soften declarations
decisions: I used my submission to attack their premises instead
consequences: No reconsideration had occurred before the later dismissal; the unused sheet remained
belief_changes: Moral indignation can preserve identity while defeating its practical objective
relationship_changes: Kappel tried to preserve options; I treated him as timid
alternative_interpretation: The committee may already have resolved to dismiss me.

title: A Number Removed
memory_text: Reuter found an arithmetic error in my summary of survival intervals, and a particularly cruel one, for it improved the apparent outcome precisely where the committee wished to see it. I could have corrected the working papers quietly, leaving the summary untouched. Instead I took a knife to the number and rewrote the page. Clara, waiting in the corridor, said that no one on the committee would have checked it. I replied that I might have. This was not a declaration of virtue. I was furious that an error of my own had provided the institution with an argument it did not deserve. The new figure made no difference to the verdict. I still remember the scraping of the knife and the clock that continued ticking while I debated whether a single honest number could cost a man his laboratory.
prior_expectations: A striking success would redeem uncertain evidence
observations: The central survival estimate failed Reuter's arithmetic check
decisions: I revised the number before the next faculty statement
consequences: The corrected result looked less spectacular and remained unpersuasive
belief_changes: I could not defend an inaccurate calculation even to save myself
relationship_changes: Reuter accepted the correction without offering comfort
source_anchors: The Lost Years v7 integrated autobiography
alternative_interpretation: Other causes for this recollection remain possible; the narrator is selective.

title: The Dismissal and the Box
locations: University of Ingolstadt and Lenz workshop
memory_text: The faculty's sentence arrived in a thick envelope bearing very little argument and a great quantity of institutional dignity. I was dismissed. Heller was absent when the matter was concluded. Kappel brought a crate lined with discarded examination papers, an arrangement which pleased me for reasons I did not care to explain. A clerk showed me a torn draft of a letter in which Henry had offered to speak in my defense. The letter had not been sent. I might have asked him why; I preferred, at the time, to despise his hesitation without hearing its cause. Clara insisted that the living vessels be carried upright. I carried my blue ledger. That evening I possessed neither laboratory nor professorship, although no committee in creation could divest me of the learning by which I had obtained them.
prior_expectations: I expected institutional hostility but still imagined an appeal might succeed
observations: The dismissal was final and several allies offered limited aid
decisions: I packed records and safeguarded living specimens
consequences: I lost position, rooms and public standing
belief_changes: Achievement does not guarantee institutional protection
relationship_changes: Kappel and Clara helped materially; Henry's silence wounded my pride without proving betrayal

title: The Coat with an Unfinished Hem
memory_text: I collected the last of my clothes from Leonie's workroom after the dismissal. My black coat hung from a nail with its hem still pinned. She said she had not finished the alteration because I had failed to arrive for the fitting on three occasions. I reminded her that my professional circumstances had become unusually complicated. She took out the pins, laid the coat upon the table, and said that a man who refused to stand still could hardly demand perfect tailoring. Clara arrived with clean linen for the tower. For a moment the two women discussed weather and mending as though my expulsion were a minor inconvenience to ordinary life. I found this intolerable. I paid Leonie in cash, although she had not asked, and left before either could offer condolences. At the tower that evening I discovered one pin remaining in the lining. I wore the coat for weeks with the point against my wrist rather than take it back. There is a difference between endurance and stupidity. On that occasion I probably crossed it.
prior_expectations: Dismissal would command the undivided attention of everyone around me
observations: Leonie and Clara continued practical work despite my disgrace
decisions: I paid and departed rather than accept ordinary care
consequences: A coat became an object linking humiliation, independence, and attachment
belief_changes: Suffering is not made more dignified by refusing an easy repair
relationship_changes: Leonie remained connected by an unfinished practical obligation
source_anchors: Source autobiography: 1860-1899, homunculi, dismissal 1868; story added as film-informed fiction
interpretation_basis: Film scholarship suggests critical themes; this event is an invented reconstructed memory

title: The One Vessel Left Behind
memory_text: There was room for one more vessel in the wagon. I had to choose between an inactive specimen in an exceptionally handsome bowl and the crate of spare stoppers Lenz insisted we would need before the winter. I chose the stoppers and announced the decision as a triumph of reason over attachment. Lenz did not look at me. He tied the crate with wet rope while I returned alone to the annex. On the bench a chalk circle showed where the bowl had stood for months. I copied the label into the blue ledger, although the last observations were several weeks old, and left the vessel where the faculty might take possession of it. I have occasionally imagined someone opening it years afterward. I have no evidence that anyone did. The empty circle was a more exact memory than any speech I prepared for that day.
prior_expectations: Every possession must be rescued from the university
observations: One inert culture would occupy precious transport space
decisions: I abandoned the inert vessel, but copied its label into the blue ledger
consequences: Loss remained without a reassuring interpretation
belief_changes: I could not carry every failure even while claiming to remember them
relationship_changes: Lenz refused my theatrical last speech and hauled the living jars
source_anchors: The Lost Years v7 integrated autobiography
alternative_interpretation: Other causes for this recollection remain possible; the narrator is selective.

title: The Tower with Three Dry Rooms
memory_text: The tower was cheaper than any respectable laboratory and possessed three rooms that remained dry in rain, a virtue sufficient to outweigh its missing stair rail. Lenz tested the upper floor with his boot and refused to carry a jar across it until the beams had been supported. I called his caution provincial. He asked whether I preferred the Queen to arrive on the ground floor by gravity. Clara brought straw, blankets and two pails whose contents were not to be confused. We moved the creatures before the books, the books before my clothes. At dusk the Queen was settled in the least draughty corner, and I discovered that my own bed was damp. I slept beside the heating stove and congratulated myself on having chosen independence.
prior_expectations: I expected a secluded tower to offer immediate liberty
observations: Structural decay threatened specimens and my comfort
decisions: I accepted Lenz's repairs and prioritized living jars
consequences: The tower became a laboratory at personal cost
belief_changes: Autonomy depends on maintenance
relationship_changes: Lenz could overrule me on safety; Clara remained a practical steward
source_anchors: continued life and observation of homunculi

title: The Price of Coal
memory_text: At the university, coal had entered the cellar by an arrangement as natural and inexplicable as Providence. At the tower it came wet, late, and at a price which might have warmed us by outrage alone. I economized on heat until the King lost appetite and the Queen grew languid.
