Clara found a box of my cigars and laid it beside the fuel bill. She was offensively silent. I disposed of the cigars and bought coal. The creatures revived, though I shall not pretend that one evening establishes a complete theory of temperature. I recorded the readings beside the expense and put the empty cigar box away. For a week afterward I found myself seeking it at the usual hour. Habit is a petty tyrant, with none of the grandeur of an emperor.
prior_expectations: I expected exile to reduce expenses
observations: Heat directly affected the creatures' activity
decisions: I bought fuel rather than cigars
consequences: A stable heat budget became indispensable
belief_changes: Life-support costs outrank ornamental comforts
relationship_changes: Clara's authority extended to daily resource allocation
source_anchors: continued life and observation of homunculi

title: The Coat on the Nail
memory_text: My professorial coat hung from a nail in the tower's stairwell because the damp made a wardrobe an architectural joke. I had worn it during the hearing and would not relinquish it merely because the university had reclaimed its keys. Clara found the lining spotted with mildew. She said she would have it dried and patched; I said the coat was perfectly serviceable. Lenz pointed out that the shoulders had begun to smell like a neglected cellar. I gave it over with a ceremony of offended dignity. Clara returned it three days later, the cuffs repaired with thread slightly darker than the original. At a time when every other article seemed to have changed its address or its owner, I found the coat in the same place each morning. I called this discipline. Clara called it a curious attachment to a poor nail. Neither description accounts for the fact that I put it on before answering official letters.
prior_expectations: Without a university title the professorial coat should cease to matter
observations: I wore the old coat when I wrote official letters, although it hung on a damp nail
decisions: I kept and used it despite calling the practice practical
consequences: The garment remained a private means of recovering authority
belief_changes: Institutional dismissal could remove office but not my performance of the office
relationship_changes: Clara and Lenz noticed an attachment I declined to name
alternative_interpretation: Habit and protection from cold can partly explain wearing it.

title: The Door That Would Not Lock
memory_text: Someone tried the tower door during a night of sleet. I heard the latch rise twice, then a boot on the step. By the time I reached the entrance no one was there. Lenz examined the lock the following morning and found it damaged by rust rather than an intruder. I disliked this explanation, for it denied me a suitably sinister enemy. He fitted a new bolt and asked why I kept a lamp burning against the window. I told him it allowed me to observe the tower's surroundings. He said it also advertised that someone was awake inside. We moved the light and installed a small shaded lantern. I did not abandon my suspicion, but for the next week I listened more carefully before naming every sound a persecutor.
prior_expectations: I expected the faculty to send someone after my records
observations: Rust explained the faulty latch better than hostile visitors
decisions: I accepted a new bolt and changed the lighting
consequences: Tower security improved without confirming a conspiracy
belief_changes: Explanations of danger need evidence
relationship_changes: Lenz could puncture my dramatic interpretations without losing my trust
source_anchors: continued life and observation of homunculi

title: A Letter from Henry
memory_text: Henry wrote from somewhere beyond my immediate reach. His letter asked after the smaller creatures and whether I had found a way to maintain viable tissue at greater scale. It contained no offer to visit. I began a reply of forty pages and reduced it to four. I sent him observations on the limits of growth but refused the procedure he sought, although I could scarcely have given him one. At the end I added a line asking whether he had recovered from the quarrels of our final university months. I struck it out and wrote instead that the Queen continued to exhibit surprising preferences. He did not answer for several years. I kept his letter under the blue ledger where it left a pale rectangular mark.
prior_expectations: I expected Henry to seek me out as a partner
observations: He wrote for information, not companionship, and later fell silent
decisions: I sent a limited technical reply
consequences: The mentorship survived as uncertain correspondence
belief_changes: Shared inquiry does not guarantee reciprocal attachment
relationship_changes: I maintained pride and private concern about Henry
source_anchors: continued life and observation of homunculi

title: A Letter without a Title
memory_text: Henry's letter had arrived in May. I had answered the technical question it contained within a week and spent another six drafting a second letter that would make him understand the larger offense done to me. Kappel visited with new paper and asked whom I intended the second document to persuade. I said Henry deserved to know how the university had punished success. Kappel asked why I had written the word 'witness' four times. I crossed it out three times and sent only the technical correction. I have never discovered whether Henry received that answer. The longer letter remained in the drawer beside his youthful anatomical sketches. I preferred to consider the correspondence an unfinished scientific exchange. The drafts suggested another possibility, one so tiresomely personal that I bound them together and labelled the packet 'administration.'
prior_expectations: A letter from Henry need only be answered on its technical merits
observations: I revised drafts that contained unnecessary personal questions
decisions: I sent a limited reply and archived the discarded pages as administration
consequences: The relationship continued through cautious correspondence rather than reunion
belief_changes: Emotional exposure can be hidden within apparent professional rigor
relationship_changes: Henry remained an important absent interlocutor
alternative_interpretation: Editing may also have reflected normal professional restraint.

title: The King Takes a Fall
memory_text: The King fell from his platform in the course of some performance meant, I presume, to impress the Queen. His gait afterward was slow. I declared that a fall of such trifling proportions could do no harm, a confident statement pronounced before I had examined him. Clara moved the furnishings nearer the floor while I prepared reasons why the original height had been sensible. The Queen remained on the side of her vessel facing him until he recovered. I shall not make a romance of it. The King promptly attempted to scale our new partition and behaved as though safety were an indignity inflicted by lesser courtiers. I almost applauded his spirit. Then I adjusted the barrier and avoided looking at Clara.
prior_expectations: I expected scaled-down bodies to tolerate familiar movements
observations: The King showed persistent impairment after a fall
decisions: I lowered platforms and installed a barrier
consequences: Safety restrictions altered the social habitat
belief_changes: Scale alone does not eliminate vulnerability
relationship_changes: Clara challenged my complacency; the King's behavior complicated proprietary pride
source_anchors: continued life and observation of homunculi

title: A Debt in Small Coins
memory_text: Lenz came to fit a glass valve and found me counting copper coins beside an untouched dish of potatoes. The university stipend had ceased. Two patrons who promised sympathy had failed to send payment. He set the valve in place and gave me a bill with the date left open. I objected that I could pay for honest work. He replied that he knew this, which was why he was willing to wait. Clara arrived later with coal and an account she refused to describe as charity. I insisted upon signing every debt in the blue ledger. They signed as witnesses, rather as though I were founding a bank. I repaid the sums, not always promptly. Years later when younger men proposed arrangements based solely upon mutual enthusiasm, I demanded a date, a price, and a means of leaving. Trust had reached me through a bill that nobody was in a hurry to collect.
prior_expectations: A supplier's patience indicates either negligence or impending leverage
observations: Lenz observed me counting coins and extended credit on usable terms
decisions: I accepted terms without public gratitude
consequences: The workshop relationship survived financial weakness
belief_changes: Trust can be established through bounded obligations rather than surrender
relationship_changes: Lenz became more than a supplier, though payment still mattered
alternative_interpretation: Lenz may have preferred a solvent future customer to personal loyalty.

title: A Letter with No Performance
memory_text: Leonie wrote to ask whether I had finally found a tailor nearer the tower. Beneath the question she noted that the municipal hall had replaced its old floorboards, rendering our first disagreement obsolete. I drafted a reply discussing the acoustical disadvantages of the replacement timber and the intellectual inadequacy of the faculty which had once used the hall. I did not send it. Instead I enclosed the coat's remaining pin in a folded paper and wrote: You were right about this. A week later she returned the pin mounted in a square of blue cloth, with a note saying she had been right about many things and expected a more informative acknowledgment if I wished to keep corresponding. I left the little parcel beside the blue ledger rather than in the drawer for worthless curiosities. Occasionally one meets a person with so little taste for deference that one is driven, against inclination, to be exact.
prior_expectations: Leonie's inquiry would demand a grand account of my disgrace
observations: She asked for a practical answer and replied to a small concession with dry humor
decisions: I sent the pin instead of a rhetorical defense
consequences: Correspondence persisted as a private relationship across exile
belief_changes: A narrow admission may preserve more dignity than a grand justification
relationship_changes: Leonie and I established a channel for unperformed exchanges
source_anchors: Source autobiography: 1860-1899, homunculi, dismissal 1868; story added as film-informed fiction
interpretation_basis: Film scholarship suggests critical themes; this event is an invented reconstructed memory

title: A Paper with No Title
memory_text: Kappel sent an unsigned packet on the restoration of interrupted processes, the pages tied without his customary green string. Someone had written in the margin, 'Ask what restores the pattern.' I imagined he wanted a paper in which I would proclaim victory over his former masters. I drafted one under a false initial and asked him to circulate it without my name. His reply was brief: 'I did not ask you to lie.' An absurdly inconvenient distinction. He had preserved my access to certain records, yet apparently expected me to preserve an ethical boundary which the university itself had never scrupled to cross. I burnt the false title page and kept the essay. It remained unfinished because I could not decide whether anonymity was prudence or surrender.
prior_expectations: I expected Kappel to help me publish anonymously
observations: His reply rejected concealment masquerading as scholarly discretion
decisions: I withdrew the false title page
consequences: The work remained private
belief_changes: Discretion differs from falsification
relationship_changes: Kappel maintained loyalty with ethical limits
source_anchors: continued life and observation of homunculi

title: A Better Failure in Winter
memory_text: I had reconstructed a promising university trial with every dimension copied from the blue ledger. It failed before the first week ended. Lenz pointed to a fern of ice upon the northern window and asked which page of my ledger mentioned the temperature of a ruined tower. I had entered the measurements of the vessel, the weight of its fittings and the hour of observation, but not the simple fact that my old laboratory was warm. The stopper had contracted and cracked. I blamed him for the glass, although the stopper was of my choosing. We replaced the vessel and repeated the observation with a different result, no more satisfactory but at least intelligible. I preserved the split stopper in the drawer marked WINTER. A foolish name, but it spared me from calling every inconvenience persecution.
prior_expectations: Repeating a lost trial would produce a lost result
observations: The tower's winter altered the behavior of an apparently identical vessel
decisions: I saved the damaged stopper and continued the trial under its new conditions
consequences: My first tower winter became a permanent disturbance in comparisons
belief_changes: The same apparatus is not the same experiment in a different room
relationship_changes: Lenz refused to call a winter failure a defect in glass
source_anchors: The Lost Years v7 integrated autobiography
alternative_interpretation: Other causes for this recollection remain possible; the narrator is selective.

title: The Chair at the Window
memory_text: I set a second chair beside the east window for Kappel's visit, though the old man seldom stayed more than half an hour. He failed to come one afternoon and then another. I left the chair in its place because it held a stack of books rather well. On the third Thursday I found myself saying aloud that his remarks about the arrangement of my index were wrong. The Queen looked up from her ledge and resumed her occupations. There was no harm in speaking to one's specimens, provided one did not mistake a movement for comprehension. When Kappel finally arrived, suffering from a cough that made the stairs laborious, I began my argument before he had removed his gloves. He asked for tea. I made it badly and was rewarded with a criticism of the leaves. It was a satisfactory hour. The chair remained by the window long after his departure, a convenience which I continued to attribute to the books.
prior_expectations: A visitor's chair is only an economical furnishing
observations: I prepared a place for Kappel that remained useful even when he had gone
decisions: I kept the second chair by the eastern window
consequences: Repeated visits acquired a durable physical location
belief_changes: An attachment can be maintained as spatial routine without being confessed
relationship_changes: Kappel came to occupy an expected place in the tower
alternative_interpretation: The chair really may have been useful for sorting books.

title: Wartime Windows
memory_text: Wagons took the road south through the summer, and every village conversation drifted toward the war with France. Lenz's brother had gone with a unit, and the glassworks had lost two trained hands. My latest vessel could not be delivered. I first treated this as an outrageous interference with science and then saw Lenz reading a letter that had passed through too many hands. We repaired what we possessed instead. I taught him my system for recording the service life of a vessel, and he taught me to mend a chipped rim without pretending it was whole. His brother survived that campaign, though we did not know it then. The delay prevented a risky transfer I had been impatient to attempt. I was not grateful to the war for this benefit.
prior_expectations: I expected supplies to follow normal arrangements
observations: War interrupted craft work and placed Lenz's family in anxiety
decisions: I postponed transfer and repaired vessels
consequences: The delay averted an untested change
belief_changes: Interruption can be protective without being desirable
relationship_changes: I saw Lenz as vulnerable beyond his usefulness
source_anchors: continued life and observation of homunculi

title: The Unbeautiful Survivor
memory_text: The ugliest thing in the cabinet endured. It was neither human nor even promisingly animal, merely an organized tangle which grew against the glass like a careless signature. Its symmetrical companions had failed long before winter. Clara moved it to the south window and covered the other empty jars with linen. I told her it was an insult to my method. She answered that it appeared to be having an exceptionally good life without consulting my opinion. One evening I caught myself making a drawing of the twisted root with uncommon care, following each detour of its outline. I did not make it beautiful. I made it exact, which gave a pleasure I had not expected. I still would not have shown it to an admirer of my miniature Queen. I was beginning to learn how many audiences I kept inside my own head.
prior_expectations: A regular shape should tolerate disturbance better
observations: A warped growth outlasted its balanced companions
decisions: I continued observing the unlovely material and refused to exhibit it
consequences: Unwanted survival undermined my ideal of graceful organization
belief_changes: Stability and symmetry were evidently poor relations
relationship_changes: Clara kept the surviving vessel by her chosen window
source_anchors: The Lost Years v7 integrated autobiography
alternative_interpretation: Other causes for this recollection remain possible; the narrator is selective.

title: The Supper Given Away
memory_text: During a lean month I preserved enough money for lamp oil by economizing on supper. Clara discovered this when she found bread hardened beside the sink and my hands shaking while I tried to set a stopcock. She said I was unfit to handle delicate glass until I had eaten. I accused her of treating me like a patient; she replied that patients occasionally possessed the sense to follow instructions. Later that evening a farm boy brought a parcel of food from Lenz's household and refused a tip. I gave him my portion of cheese for the road, then regretted it before he reached the gate. I ate the bread and preserved the lamps. There was no nobility in the transaction. The following day my hands were steady and the experiment behaved. I began keeping provisions near the workroom, which I represented to visitors as a contribution to experimental reliability rather than obedience to Clara.
prior_expectations: Missing meals is a private sacrifice with no social consequences
observations: Clara noticed insufficient food and enforced a practical adjustment
decisions: I accepted the kitchen changes while redescribing them as efficiency
consequences: The tower's procedures began to protect my physical maintenance
belief_changes: Care can be accepted under an engineering description
relationship_changes: Clara acquired sustained influence over domestic routine
alternative_interpretation: The new routine may primarily have improved experimental endurance.

title: The New Empire on Cheap Paper
memory_text: Clara brought news of the German Empire printed on paper so thin that daylight showed through the ink. She expected me to make an offensive remark and I obliged. Yet she had not come for an argument about emperors. The new postal arrangements might make some scientific correspondence easier; the price of coal had risen again. We calculated accounts while the Archbishop knocked his staff against the glass in the next room. She asked what I proposed to call my private kingdom. I said that I had no wish to rule. The Queen chose that moment to turn her back upon me, and Clara folded the newspaper without smiling. I entered the coal price in the blue ledger beneath a grander heading than it deserved.
prior_expectations: I expected imperial politics to provide only another argument
observations: Economic changes mattered more immediately than symbolic authority
decisions: I recalculated supply commitments
consequences: The tower's routine adjusted to national changes
belief_changes: Political events are lived through material details
relationship_changes: Clara's ability to puncture pretension remained welcome and irritating
source_anchors: continued life and observation of homunculi

title: The Chamber Too Large
memory_text: We spent five days constructing a vessel proportioned for a figure ten times the customary size. I had drawn it beautifully, and had consulted Lenz about every pressure and joint. We had neglected to consult the stairway. The chamber passed through the workshop door and lodged at the turn above the first landing, where it remained like a very expensive coffin. Lenz measured the clear width again while I proposed taking down a section of stone. He refused to work upon the wall without an engineer. In the end we disassembled the apparatus in the rain and carried it upward in pieces, where the rebuilt frame proved less true than before. I entered its cost under INFRASTRUCTURE, an ugly word for an ugly afternoon. I have since measured the route of every apparatus before admiring its dimensions.
prior_expectations: Enlargement of the container would permit enlargement of the subject
observations: The experimental chamber could not pass the tower stair
decisions: I dismantled the frame rather than widen the stairwell
consequences: Scale-up became a problem of architecture before physiology
belief_changes: Nature has no respect for plans that cannot cross a threshold
relationship_changes: Lenz recorded my mistake without raising his voice
source_anchors: The Lost Years v7 integrated autobiography
alternative_interpretation: Other causes for this recollection remain possible; the narrator is selective.

title: A Name Lost in the Lists
memory_text: Reuter asked me to inspect a series of records from men returning wounded after the war. One young assistant had been known to him by a nickname, yet the hospital's transfer lists had entered three different spellings of his name. The man's injury was visible; his subsequent whereabouts were not. I argued with the clerk over the mistaken initials until he permitted us to copy the surviving records. We located the assistant at another infirmary two days later. Reuter called it good fortune. I called it a victory over defective classification. The man himself was more interested in finding his spectacles than in our triumph. Clara supplied a pair from a drawer of abandoned possessions. I saw how an error in a ledger could turn an identifiable person into an administrative absence. The blue ledger acquired a separate index for those who handled or cared for my creatures. I did not call it sentimental.
prior_expectations: A clinical list need include only diagnostic and experimental details
observations: Reuter's war records showed the harm done by unacknowledged or anonymous helpers
decisions: I added the names of carers and handlers to my index
consequences: Other people's contributions became more traceable in my records
belief_changes: A life history has custodians and witnesses, not only subjects
relationship_changes: Reuter's humanitarian perspective altered my archival procedure
alternative_interpretation: The added names also simplified later verification.

title: The Queen's Quiet Week
memory_text: For six days the Queen scarcely moved. I inspected her vessel with the mortifying caution of a man whose entire theory of life might be refuted by a creature the size of a nail. Clara sat nearby reading a catalogue aloud, a droning account of roots and leaves. The Queen approached the wall nearest her voice. I said it was coincidence. Clara agreed with suspicious readiness and continued reading. In the following weeks the Queen sometimes approached certain voices, sometimes turned away. I could have staged a demonstration for visitors and announced that she knew us. Instead I moved my chair closer and kept accounts of the failures as well. There are secrets which an impatient scientist destroys merely by announcing their discovery.
prior_expectations: I expected diminished activity to signify illness
observations: The Queen approached Clara's voice without a controlled causal test
decisions: I prolonged observation rather than intervene
consequences: A possible social or acoustic preference entered the ledger
belief_changes: Not every suggestive correlation merits a confident conclusion
relationship_changes: Clara became a reassuring presence to the Queen and to me in different ways
source_anchors: continued life and observation of homunculi

title: The New Offence
locations: Tower kitchen and Ingolstadt post office
memory_text: The new imperial criminal code arrived in the district wrapped in all the language of administrative progress. Paragraph 175 was short enough to fit upon a scrap of paper. I copied its wording and placed the copy beside an older Bavarian legal digest, then spent the afternoon demonstrating to Clara that an empire could take an act previously outside that particular criminal prohibition and manufacture an offender by printing a sentence. She replied that a gentleman with a tower could afford certain sorts of indignation more readily than a clerk with a family. At the post office a man was asked, within my hearing, why he received so many letters from the same address. Nothing came of the question. I remembered it nevertheless. That evening I sealed a letter to Theodor, intending only to tell him of the changed statute. I did not post it. I was angry at the law, and somewhat angrier that my first impulse had been to imagine my old companion in danger, rather than to ask whether he was content.
prior_expectations: The new imperial code represented neutral administrative unification
observations: The statute criminalized conduct previously outside that Bavarian prohibition
decisions: I copied the provision and left an old letter unsent
consequences: Legal risk and lost affection became associated with one object
belief_changes: State classifications could create rather than merely describe danger
relationship_changes: I worried about Theodor while refusing to contact him
source_anchors: Original autobiography: pre-reunion chronology and boundary, fictional authority
v6 baseline: preserved surrounding scenes and relationships
New adult interpersonal incident: reconstructed fiction, no original source citation
Historical: Bavaria 1813 legal exception and German Reich 1871 Paragraph 175, https://www.servat.unibe.ch/dfr/bv006389.html
alternative_interpretation: His objection to state intrusion may have reflected general libertarian instincts

title: A Voice Without a Stage
memory_text: Leonie came to the tower after a dispute with the theatre manager, bringing a small box of stage pins and the curious exhaustion of a person who has been treated as indispensable and underpaid in the same hour. I displayed the Queen, who was not inclined to entertain anyone that day. Leonie watched her sit motionless in a corner, then announced that this was the most honest performance she had attended all season. Clara put soup upon the table. For once I did not lecture. Leonie spoke of a singer whose voice had failed, an apprentice who had married badly, and a room whose roof leaked upon the musicians. She asked whether I was happy in the tower. I said it was peaceful. She asked whether I was happy. I poured more soup and informed her that the question had not improved through repetition. She did not pursue it. After they left, I moved the Queen's jar from the cabinet to the table and sat where Leonie had sat. This was an alteration to my working arrangements, not a confession.
prior_expectations: A visitor would require a demonstration to justify the journey
observations: Leonie chose conversation and noticed the Queen's refusal to perform
decisions: I abandoned the planned display and preserved the seat arrangement afterward
consequences: Solitude acquired measurable interruptions by trusted companions
belief_changes: Not every encounter is improved by turning it into an exhibition
relationship_changes: Leonie became a companion without acquiring access to my private admissions
source_anchors: Source autobiography: 1860-1899, homunculi, dismissal 1868; story added as film-informed fiction
interpretation_basis: Film scholarship suggests critical themes; this event is an invented reconstructed memory

title: The Queen's Evening
memory_text: After the Queen's summer quiet spell, I began checking her platform before extinguishing the final lamp. At first I did so to determine whether her preferred position varied with the fall of light. One evening Clara watched me move the small screen, warm the outer glass with my palm, and place a scrap of bright cloth where the Queen had once selected it. 'You always do that in that order,' she said. I had not noticed. I replied that established methods deserve repetition. Clara asked whether I had tested another order. I said there was no reason to disturb a successful arrangement. The Queen settled near the cloth. I recorded nothing in the scientific column that night. What had begun as a control condition had become a ceremony whose interruption made me impatient. I retained it because the little creature appeared to prosper, not because I wished to be required at a particular hour.
prior_expectations: The Queen's evening condition can be checked whenever convenient
observations: Her behavior shifted after a quiet period and repeated nightly attention
decisions: I established a fixed end-of-day observation
consequences: My workday acquired a small ritual dependent on her welfare
belief_changes: Monitoring and attachment can arise from the same repeated act
relationship_changes: The Queen became a daily obligation, not merely a triumph
alternative_interpretation: The routine could be motivated solely by scientific caution.

title: The Festival I Did Not Attend
memory_text: Lenz invited me to his family's winter gathering. I declined because the Mermaid's water was changing color and I could not bear to leave the tower. By evening the color had returned to normal. I could have gone, but I remained with my notebook and a plate of hard cheese. On Monday Clara brought the uneaten end of a cake and said Lenz had saved it for me. I informed her that attendance at festivities was not a professional obligation. She replied that nobody had suggested it was. The cake was surprisingly good. I sent Lenz a small repair instrument in return but never admitted that I had wanted to hear his family quarrel over cards.
prior_expectations: I expected a specimen irregularity to justify isolation
observations: The problem resolved before the gathering, yet I stayed away
decisions: I sent a practical gift instead of visiting
consequences: Another ordinary invitation passed unused
belief_changes: Solitude is sometimes selected after its reason has disappeared
relationship_changes: Lenz offered friendship without work; I responded obliquely
source_anchors: continued life and observation of homunculi

title: The Undertaker's Bad Latin
memory_text: I met Georg Eberle because he had placed an advertisement offering obsolete glass for sale and I misread his occupation. He was sexton and caretaker of the old cemetery, not an instrument dealer. He showed me a row of cloudy vessels recovered from a chapel storeroom, then a register whose Latin headings had been copied incorrectly for twenty years. I corrected one. He thanked me and asked whether the correction made anyone less dead. I said it might make their survivors less misinformed, which seemed reason enough. Georg had one short leg and went down the cemetery steps sideways, neither apologizing for his gait nor requesting assistance. He offered the use of a dry undercroft for examining old stonework, provided I touched no grave and paid for my own candles. This was a remarkably sound contract. I bought the glass, though most was useless, and returned three weeks later with the proper Latin headings written on stiff card. He adopted them without admitting that this had pleased him. I understood the procedure.
prior_expectations: A cemetery keeper would be superstitious or uneducated
observations: Georg valued accurate records and negotiated practical conditions
decisions: I corrected the register and bought the glass
consequences: A recurring alliance began in a place associated with death
belief_changes: Precision can matter to the living without altering the dead
relationship_changes: Mutual respect developed through plain transactions
source_anchors: Source autobiography: 1860-1899, homunculi, dismissal 1868; story added as film-informed fiction
interpretation_basis: Film scholarship suggests critical themes; this event is an invented reconstructed memory

title: A Child with the Wrong Question
memory_text: Lenz's little daughter was permitted to see a drawing of the King, not the actual glass vessel, since her father believed my laboratory unsuitable for children. She asked why the King was made so small. I described the advantages of observing life within controlled limits. She asked why he could not come out. I explained scale, temperature, and the dangers of a careless world. She considered this and said that a bird kept in a narrow cage might also be easy to observe. Her father told her not to be rude. I assured him I had been insulted more intelligently by older people. That evening I drafted a plan for a room-sized enclosure and found the expense intolerable. I put the drawing away. For some months thereafter I found myself staring at the glass rather than through it. It would be inaccurate to say the child's question changed my convictions. It did alter the location at which the discomfort appeared.
prior_expectations: A child will admire the cleverness of an artificial royal creature
observations: Anna asked about the King in terms that unsettled my assumptions
decisions: I restricted the visit to a drawing but kept reflecting upon the question
consequences: The discomfort recurred in later discussions of care for created lives
belief_changes: Other perspectives can reveal questions that the maker's pride overlooks
relationship_changes: I began treating Anna's questions as serious despite her youth
alternative_interpretation: The discomfort need not amount to a changed ethical position.

title: An Inventory of Small Preferences
memory_text: I entered my six little subjects in the blue ledger with their principal inclinations: the Queen's ledge, the King's devotion, the Archbishop's interruptions, the Devil's mirror, the Ballerina's music, and the Mermaid's preference for seclusion. It was an elegant chart. Clara ruined it by adding a column for exceptions. The Ballerina would not always dance in the cold; the Devil forgot his reflection when the King was active; the Mermaid appeared in bright light if nobody approached. I demanded that the exceptions be measured properly, and for three days no work of immediate ambition was done. The table became more useful and decidedly uglier. I retained it. A monarch, a devil, and a dancing girl had contrived to make a fool of the neatest account of their characters.
prior_expectations: I expected stable preferences to be enough for prediction
observations: Context-dependent exceptions appeared in every individual
decisions: I accepted an exception column
consequences: The creatures became subjects of longitudinal comparison
belief_changes: Identity includes variability and context
relationship_changes: Clara strengthened her role as critical co-observer
source_anchors: continued life and observation of homunculi

title: The Queen's False Silence
memory_text: A young physician declared that the Queen had grown dull. She remained motionless for his inspection and moved freely an hour after he had gone. I described her recovery to Clara, who asked whether the creature might be tired of us. Naturally I replied that fatigue had not been established. Still, I moved the clock, dismissed callers, and watched from behind a screen until the afternoon light changed. The Queen climbed her ledge, made an orderly circuit and returned to her customary corner. I had learned a valuable caution and felt very little satisfaction in it. A genius whose proof depends upon a subject appearing on command owns not a discovery but a small theatre with an unreliable performer. I did not entirely abandon the theatre.
prior_expectations: The Queen's stillness signified decline
observations: A visitor's sharp voice coincided with her withdrawal
decisions: I arranged a period without visitors and watched through a screen
consequences: Silence became an ambiguous response rather than an empty datum
belief_changes: Absence of display need not mean absence of life
relationship_changes: Voss began objecting whenever I claimed the Queen had performed
source_anchors: The Lost Years v7 integrated autobiography
alternative_interpretation: Other causes for this recollection remain possible; the narrator is selective.

title: A Printer's Daughter
memory_text: A bookseller sent me to the Rosen shop because its proprietor would accept an order that respectable printers declined. I expected an old conspirator and found his daughter Mathilde removing type from a forme with fingers black to the second joint. She had read the unsigned paper I had circulated and identified a numeral reproduced incorrectly in three places. Her father, she said, would print anything provided the customer paid, but she preferred a manuscript that knew the difference between seven and seventeen. I suggested that no intelligent reader could have mistaken my meaning. She set both numbers beside one another in metal type. Under the shop's hard northern light I saw how very little intelligence a reader required to ruin a result. I ordered thirty private copies and forbade her to improve my punctuation. The corrected numeral was hers, though the cover carried only my initials.
prior_expectations: I expected a compliant trade service
observations: Mathilde spotted an arithmetical error before the printing
decisions: I commissioned a corrected private edition
consequences: The private paper became legible and an independent editorial relationship began
belief_changes: Practical accuracy could come from outside the academy
relationship_changes: Mathilde earned technical respect without receiving my patronage
source_anchors: All new supporting people, events, dates, and dialogue are reconstructed

title: Dinner Among the Stones
memory_text: Rain detained me in Georg's undercroft while I waited for a mason to bring measurements of a sealed arch. The mason never arrived. I had bread, pickled onions, a tin of sardines, and a bottle which Georg identified as a respectable gin only after he tasted it. Leonie appeared looking for the caretaker to whom she had promised two repaired funeral hangings. She stopped at the sight of our supper spread across a broad stone lid and accused me of selecting my dining companions for their inability to contradict me. Georg, very much alive, contradicted her immediately. She sat on a folded sack and ate an onion. We discussed roof repairs, funeral fees, and the absurd custom of spending a dead man's remaining money upon a monument larger than his house. The damp made my fingers ache. I remember laughing at something Georg said, although not what it was. There was no ceremony and no triumph. On later solitary visits, a meal among tombs seemed entirely natural. A sensible location is not invalidated by its reputation.
prior_expectations: A cemetery was unsuitable for ordinary human company
observations: Georg and Leonie made an improvised meal companionable
decisions: I returned to the undercroft for work and occasionally food
consequences: Dining in a mortuary setting became an unforced habit
belief_changes: A macabre setting can be domestic when its users know it well
relationship_changes: Georg and Leonie entered the same circle without formal introduction
source_anchors: Source autobiography: 1860-1899, homunculi, dismissal 1868; story added as film-informed fiction
interpretation_basis: Film scholarship suggests critical themes; this event is an invented reconstructed memory

title: The Price of a Name
memory_text: On collecting the copies I found one sheet laid aside, a proof headed with my full name. Mathilde had set it to see whether my initials occupied less space. They did not. Kappel, who had accompanied me on the unlikely pretext of buying envelopes, asked whether I wished to hide the argument or its author. An offensive distinction, particularly when delivered before a printer's daughter. I told him that a signed statement would give the faculty another occasion to pronounce upon things they could neither measure nor mend. Mathilde asked why, in that event, I had placed my address beneath the final paragraph. I had meant to invite correspondence. I removed the address from twenty copies and preserved it on ten. I received one hostile letter and two requests for particulars, all sent to Kappel, who claimed this vindicated the experiment in honesty.
prior_expectations: I expected anonymity to preserve both priority and privacy
observations: A concealed byline coexisted badly with a contact address
decisions: I split the copies into two distributions
consequences: Responses made the cost of authorship measurable
belief_changes: Concealment and recognition were competing aims
relationship_changes: Kappel and Mathilde learned where to press an argument I preferred to evade
source_anchors: All new supporting people, events, dates, and dialogue are reconstructed

title: An Invoice for Silence
memory_text: Mathilde had completed a small private impression of my experimental notes. She offered to omit the shop's mark from the final copies if I paid for the additional work. I asked whether secrecy carried a tariff. She said so did paper, type, and the risk of explaining a mysterious order to a magistrate. Kappel, examining a proof, suggested that a few copies be given to credible witnesses rather than hidden in cupboards. I disliked the notion that I needed witnesses and ordered twelve extra copies. Mathilde kept one sealed in her shop, with a date and a list of corrections. I objected to her retaining my work. She replied that a printer who cannot prove what he printed is a convenient scapegoat. Years later I would say that no university deserved to control my name. When a date was disputed years later, Mathilde produced her sealed proof without troubling to look pleased.
prior_expectations: A discreet printer should omit my name to preserve anonymity
observations: Mathilde demanded accountable attribution and a usable record
decisions: I allowed my name to be handled under agreed printing controls
consequences: The edition created a new category of trusted professional collaborator
belief_changes: Public identity requires custody, not merely concealment
relationship_changes: Mathilde became a keeper of my evidence and reputation
alternative_interpretation: Mathilde also had an ordinary commercial stake in accuracy.

title: The Old Automaton
memory_text: Mathilde arrived carrying Hoffmann's tale of the Sandman and a mechanical bird whose owner had tired of winding it. She regarded the doll Olympia as a rather transparent indictment of men who prefer agreeable women to attentive ones. Lenz opened the bird and showed us a spring worn almost smooth where the mechanism failed to catch. I proposed that a genuinely living creature must repair some portion of its own disturbance. Mathilde pointed out that people also required repairs from others; she tapped Lenz's old burn scar without asking permission. We set the bird upon the window ledge, and its beak moved three times before falling silent. The King meanwhile knocked upon his partition until the Archbishop turned away. I disliked how easily the company transferred its attention from a machine to my little court, but I was not foolish enough to demand an explanation from a bird.
prior_expectations: I expected the literary automaton to confirm my distinction between mechanism and life
observations: Wear and social dependence complicated the easy contrast
decisions: I observed both bird and homunculi without demonstrating either
consequences: The repaired bird became a recurring control object
belief_changes: Autonomy cannot be defined by motion alone
relationship_changes: Mathilde's criticism of agreeable puppets altered our conversations
source_anchors: All new supporting people, events, dates, and dialogue are reconstructed

title: The Doctor in the Funeral Book
memory_text: Georg discovered that the dates recorded for a retired physician differed between a burial register and a charitable hospital's accounts. Reuter offered to check the hospital entry. I dismissed the discrepancy as a clerk's ordinary incompetence until the supposed physician's widow came to complain that a pension had ceased a month before his death. Dates, which are so tedious when accurate, become suddenly fascinating when someone earns money by altering them. Reuter found the hospital copy intact. Georg found the cemetery entry had been scraped and rewritten. I took impressions of the damaged paper, a labor requiring more patience than ingenuity. We could not identify who had made the alteration, but the widow obtained a hearing. Georg thanked Reuter and me with the same expression, which was almost an insult. I had come to study preservation of tissue, yet the decisive instrument that week was a dull pencil rubbed across a slip of paper. I later bought a better set of graphite sticks and pretended they were for laboratory diagrams.
prior_expectations: A one-month discrepancy in a burial record was harmless
observations: The discrepancy affected a widow's pension and the register had been altered
decisions: I helped preserve the physical evidence
consequences: Record integrity gained practical as well as scientific importance
belief_changes: Minor falsification can propagate into another person's life
relationship_changes: I respected Georg's insistence upon accurate names and dates
source_anchors: Source autobiography: 1860-1899, homunculi, dismissal 1868; story added as film-informed fiction
interpretation_basis: Film scholarship suggests critical themes; this event is an invented reconstructed memory

title: A Patient without a Name
memory_text: Reuter invited me to review records of a patient who had repeatedly recovered after periods of apparently profound unresponsiveness. I went by a roundabout route, avoiding people who knew my dismissal. The patient was an elderly man who liked chess and disliked being spoken of as a case while present. Reuter introduced me as an old university colleague, neither defending nor condemning me. I asked the man whether he remembered the intervals. He remembered waking and finding the room changed, but nothing of what had happened between. I left with notes less triumphant than I had hoped. Reuter sent me away with a packet of clean linen for the tower. He had noticed that my cuffs were fraying. This small evidence of attention remained with me.
prior_expectations: I expected clinical recovery to establish a sharp threshold of life
observations: The patient's report and records left important gaps
decisions: I interviewed him respectfully and revised my notes
consequences: The collaboration resumed under discreet terms
belief_changes: Memory absence is not proof of nonexistence or death
relationship_changes: Reuter extended human regard without endorsing my work
source_anchors: continued life and observation of homunculi

title: The Borrowed Name
memory_text: Mathilde introduced me to Max Reiss, a schoolteacher who wished to have a short defense of a dismissed colleague printed without identifying the author. Reiss was careful with his verbs and almost reckless with the number of copies he proposed to circulate. I asked whether the colleague had broken the law. He said that he did not know, and that the allegation had preceded any examination. Mathilde declined to print a name without the man's consent. I proposed a general argument about accusations unsupported by evidence and spent three nights correcting it. Reiss thought the piece too cold to influence the public. Mathilde said that my colder language might keep the teacher employed. We printed fewer copies than Reiss wanted. Weeks later he reported that the school had quietly ceased asking questions. I claimed no victory; no public correction had appeared. What I retained was Mathilde's insistence that the person concerned should choose how much of himself the pamphlet spent.
prior_expectations: Anonymous publication would best protect everyone involved
observations: Reiss and Mathilde disagreed over circulation and consent
decisions: I revised the argument and accepted fewer copies
consequences: I learned the cost of using others as evidence
belief_changes: A target's preferences mattered in defensive publication
relationship_changes: Mathilde and Reiss became trusted, independently minded collaborators
source_anchors: Original autobiography: pre-reunion chronology and boundary, fictional authority
v6 baseline: preserved surrounding scenes and relationships
New adult interpersonal incident: reconstructed fiction, no original source citation
alternative_interpretation: Prudence rather than respect may explain limited distribution

title: A Patient's Complaint
memory_text: The patient whose unusual periods of insensibility had interested me returned while I was visiting Reuter. He had become quite recovered and wished to know why a stranger had been shown particulars of his treatment. Reuter explained that I was a scientific consultant. The patient asked whether this entitled me to write about his body. I assured him the notes bore no name. He pointed to his occupation and age, which narrowed the possibilities in the town to perhaps three men. I had regarded anonymity as a mechanical matter of removing letters. Reuter asked me to correct the report before circulation, and I did, though I resented the time. Afterward I removed occupations from other case notes where they contributed nothing to the phenomenon. I remained convinced that useful knowledge ought not perish for want of access. I removed two unnecessary particulars from the next report. The pen nearly tore the page where I pressed too hard.
prior_expectations: Clinical access granted once can be renewed without confronting the patient
observations: The subject objected to the way his condition had been described
decisions: I revised how the case could be discussed with Reuter
consequences: The limits of my authority became part of continuing clinical correspondence
belief_changes: An observational right can lapse when those observed contest it
relationship_changes: Reuter's patient became more than a data point in the relationship
alternative_interpretation: Fear of lost medical access may explain part of the concession.

title: A Door with Two Accounts
memory_text: Clara lent her rear table for a meeting with Mathilde because the printshop's landlord had developed an appetite for listening through walls. Her dispensary ledger lay open at the edge of the table, each unpaid bottle entered against a name. Mathilde wanted to publish a clear description of the homunculi, including the circumstances under which they refused to move. Clara asked whether the report would expose them to visitors. I said a glass vessel could not be injured by the attention of a gentleman who understood glass. Both women looked at me until I amended the claim to the animals within it. We discussed paper dimensions instead. Clara measured her charges by what they could bear; Mathilde by what could be read; I by what could be proved. We reached no philosophy that afternoon. We agreed, rather less nobly, to use numbers instead of names in any public account.
prior_expectations: I expected publication concerns to be solved by anonymity
observations: Clara distinguished public curiosity from a creature's welfare
decisions: I substituted anonymized observations for an exhibition proposal
consequences: The publishing plan acquired a boundary that survived later disputes
belief_changes: Demonstration and publicity carry separate risks
relationship_changes: Clara and Mathilde became collaborators without becoming my disciples
source_anchors: All new supporting people, events, dates, and dialogue are reconstructed

title: The Living Specimen and the Silk
memory_text: Mathilde came with a proof of my account of miniature differentiation. I had described a series of splendid appearances, each one supported by precise adjectives and very little troublesome arithmetic. She tapped the passage in which I called two vessels successful, then placed beside it the record showing that both had ceased to respond. I asked whether a printer was now to adjudicate viability. She said a reader would do so if I gave him the opportunity. We worked through a rainy evening replacing my most handsome sentences with measurements and the names of failures. When I saw the result in type it had lost something of my elegance. It had gained the inconvenient property of being a document I could consult without remembering which claims I had embellished. We kept a copy beside the ledger.
prior_expectations: Describing an experiment elegantly would secure its scientific reception
observations: Mathilde found my prose concealed two failures
decisions: I restored the failed observations and shortened the boast
consequences: The pamphlet became less persuasive and more durable
belief_changes: Style cannot carry a result unsupported by its records
relationship_changes: Mathilde took charge of marking disputed claims in the margins
source_anchors: The Lost Years v7 integrated autobiography
alternative_interpretation: Other causes for this recollection remain possible; the narrator is selective.

title: The Saint Who Refused the Bottle
memory_text: Georg's cousin Matthias, a priest with uneven spectacles and a ruined umbrella, discovered me examining a damaged memorial near the gatehouse. He asked whether my work in the tower resembled the stories circulating about it. I offered him gin and the distinction between a story and evidence. He declined the gin, accepted the distinction, and asked to see an observation book. I produced one which contained no secrets of preparation, merely measurements. He spent half an hour asking questions of surprising pertinence. Then he said that if the little beings could suffer, my obligations to them might be greater, not less, than a parent's obligations to a child. I observed that parenthood was an analogy with considerable sentimental baggage. He replied that I had chosen to use the analogy of creation in the first place. I disliked the conversation. I invited him to return when I had less time to waste. He did not interpret this as refusal. His spectacles were repaired before his next visit. I was almost disappointed.
prior_expectations: A priest would rely upon condemnation rather than serious inquiry
observations: Matthias asked about observation and responsibility without demanding orthodoxy
decisions: I permitted him access to limited evidence
consequences: A durable adversarial relationship began across theological differences
belief_changes: Religious office does not preclude precise argument
relationship_changes: Matthias became an unwelcome but respected critic
source_anchors: Source autobiography: 1860-1899, homunculi, dismissal 1868; story added as film-informed fiction
interpretation_basis: Film scholarship suggests critical themes; this event is an invented reconstructed memory

title: The Train Compartment
memory_text: Lenz and I travelled by rail to collect an optical fitting. He insisted on facing forward and devoured sandwiches while I suffered the indignities of the carriage's motion. A little girl asked whether our case contained a bird; Lenz said it contained a thing considerably more troublesome. I was charmed until she demanded that we open it. At the workshop we discovered they had repaired the wrong fitting. I gave the proprietor an account of incompetence which ought to have been published for the benefit of craftsmen throughout Europe. Lenz produced the original order with its number and obtained a correction in four sentences. On the return journey he wrote that number inside the case. I permitted it. I did not permit him to describe the whole day as wasted, because we had acquired an excellent story at the proprietor's expense.
prior_expectations: I expected the journey to solve an equipment problem
observations: A vendor confused fittings and Lenz's practical method was more effective than anger
decisions: I accepted a corrected order
consequences: The failure improved our procurement routine
belief_changes: Administrative precision is a scientific tool
relationship_changes: Lenz became a counterweight to my impulsive contempt
source_anchors: continued life and observation of homunculi

title: The Parcel Not Opened
memory_text: A parcel marked with Kappel's hand arrived damp and partly crushed. I assumed it contained another catalogue of obscure dissertations and left it under the stairs while I dealt with a failed preparation. Three days later Lenz used the box to prop open a door. Kappel arrived and asked whether I had read the letter within. It concerned an offer of privately held instruments whose owner would accept a visit only before the end of the month. We had missed the opportunity. I accused the rain, the messenger, and Lenz's mechanical ingenuity. Kappel asked why none of them had prevented my opening the parcel. I dislike questions which have only one answer and are therefore disguised accusations. I thereafter sorted letters by the sender's handwriting before attending to their scientific subject. Some senders mattered because of their knowledge. Others mattered because they would be offended, or absent, if neglected long enough.
prior_expectations: A wet and damaged parcel has no personal meaning apart from its contents
observations: Kappel's familiar handwriting made the unopened bundle difficult to ignore
decisions: I dried and kept it rather than discard it unread
consequences: The handwriting became a cue for the relationship beyond its informational value
belief_changes: Custody of a person's work can masquerade as purely practical interest
relationship_changes: Kappel remained important as a correspondent rather than a provider alone
alternative_interpretation: The papers may have been genuinely valuable to the archive.

title: The Volume without a Spine
memory_text: Kappel brought out a bound collection of withdrawn anatomical reports, its spine removed to avoid a title on the shelf. Between two accounts of failed grafts lay a memorandum I remembered arguing against as a student. I now found its descriptions of interrupted recovery remarkably sound. Mathilde, who had come to inspect the paper stock, asked why I had underlined the author's error but not his correct prediction. I told her that mistakes invite marks more urgently than commonplaces. She put a small cross beside the neglected passage. Later, alone, I compared it with three records from the Queen's early months. The resemblance was insufficient for a conclusion and sufficiently irritating to occupy my Christmas holiday. I copied the memorandum, leaving its author's name intact. Kappel noticed. He said nothing, which was the most agreeable compliment I ever received from him.
prior_expectations: I expected the rejected volume to contain cautionary mistakes
observations: A dismissed predecessor had made one defensible prediction
decisions: I copied the memorandum with attribution
consequences: An old adversary entered my working archive
belief_changes: Institutional rejection does not make every rejected inference correct or false
relationship_changes: Kappel granted quiet approval; Mathilde pressed attribution
source_anchors: All new supporting people, events, dates, and dialogue are reconstructed

title: The Devil at Vespers
memory_text: Matthias asked me to look at a heating pipe in his church because Georg thought the metal had been installed improperly. I attended after vespers, when the last parishioners were collecting their shawls. A painted devil above the doorway had been restored so clumsily that he appeared to be smiling at the congregation. I remarked that he was the only figure on the wall enjoying himself. Matthias said the artisan had meant to express malice and was merely incompetent. We examined the pipe and found a leak where condensation had softened the plaster. Georg fetched a bucket. I was obliged to stand upon the church's ladder while the priest steadied its feet. From above I could see the painted saint and devil together, each accusing the other of bad company. I thought of the black-caped figure in my laboratory and resolved to inspect him more closely when I returned. Matthias asked whether I had formed a new opinion of the church. I said its plumbing was abominable. He admitted that this was now beyond dispute.
prior_expectations: Sacred imagery would provide easy material for mockery
observations: The priest accepted practical criticism and helped solve the heating problem
decisions: I inspected the pipe and later compared the painted devil with my figure
consequences: Religious opposition acquired ordinary texture and comic flexibility
belief_changes: A disagreeable institution may contain competent individuals
relationship_changes: Matthias and I developed a form of cooperative argument
source_anchors: Source autobiography: 1860-1899, homunculi, dismissal 1868; story added as film-informed fiction
interpretation_basis: Film scholarship suggests critical themes; this event is an invented reconstructed memory

title: The Archbishop Changes Sides
memory_text: The Archbishop, long the King's adversary, surprised me by standing between the King and a falling piece of miniature furniture. I first thought the gesture accidental. Then he helped push the object against the wall. The King spent the evening beside him rather than beside the Queen. I watched this unlikely truce until the lamp oil failed. Clara urged me not to describe a single cooperative action as reconciliation. I obeyed in writing and disobeyed in conversation. By the end of the month the two had returned to their usual disputes, but sometimes shared a ledge without quarrelling. I made a new observation card instead of erasing the old one. Their history had developed complications inconvenient to a simple allegory.
prior_expectations: I expected the Archbishop to oppose the King in every context
observations: Cooperation occurred during a physical hazard
decisions: I created a separate relationship record
consequences: Their antagonism became conditional rather than absolute
belief_changes: Relationships are histories, not fixed labels
relationship_changes: Clara moderated my tendency to dramatize every exception
source_anchors: continued life and observation of homunculi

title: The Archbishop's Audience
memory_text: Mathilde asked to see the beings about which she had been setting type for eighteen months. I permitted the visit at noon, when the light was steady, and arranged the Archbishop's chamber nearest the table. The little ecclesiastic stood motionless until the King stumbled against a narrow ledge. He then crossed the enclosure and laid one hand upon the rail, an act that looked wonderfully like assistance and might equally have been possession of a favored object. Mathilde whispered, with exasperating delight, that my bishop had better instincts than some professors. I wished to correct her, but the King was already upright. I wrote the precise order of movement, and Lenz quietly widened the dangerous ledge while my guest was examining the Queen. She left without demanding proof of souls. She did request that I remove the word 'obedient' from the printer's proof.
prior_expectations: I expected the Archbishop to perform his customary disapproval
observations: His approach coincided with the King's recovery
decisions: I documented the sequence and permitted a structural repair
consequences: The next printed account omitted an unearned claim of obedience
belief_changes: Purpose cannot be read directly from a gesture
relationship_changes: Mathilde became a trusted but critical witness to the homunculi
source_anchors: All new supporting people, events, dates, and dialogue are reconstructed

title: The Archbishop's Place
memory_text: Mathilde returned to observe the little Archbishop, who had recently surprised us by protecting rather than obstructing the King. She wanted a clean account of the change for the next impression of my notes. I offered a theory of rank and allegiance. Clara remarked that the Archbishop had stood where the strongest current of warm air entered the vessel, and that his position may have had nothing to do with the King. We arranged another observation and found that both explanations fit some of the movements. Mathilde set the paragraph with the words 'cannot presently distinguish.' I ordered them removed, then restored them when she asked which experiment would permit a stronger claim. I liked the Archbishop better after that. Whether he possessed loyalty, preference for warmth, or merely a talent for deceiving me, he had earned his place in the account without requesting permission from my theory.
prior_expectations: The Archbishop should retain his role as disapproving adversary
observations: New observations showed him behaving differently from the role I assigned
decisions: I allowed Mathilde's discrepant observations into the record
consequences: The creature's changed behavior complicated my preferred theatrical categories
belief_changes: Living conduct should not always conform to the creator's cast list
relationship_changes: Mathilde became a witness willing to contradict my narrative
alternative_interpretation: The apparent protection might have arisen from warmth or chance.

title: A Review Written in Advance
memory_text: An editor from Augsburg returned our prospectus with the assurance that claims of miniature men could be dismissed without an inspection. He had, however, complimented my literary manner, which showed him capable of good judgment in a narrow field. Mathilde had already composed a rebuttal before I arrived. She proposed to print the rejection beside an inventory of witnessed behaviors. I advised her that humiliation was more effective when administered sparingly; she replied that I had furnished enough for a lifetime. We quarrelled over whether the editor's name belonged on the sheet. She wished to print it. I did not wish to give a mediocrity the immortality of appearing in my pamphlet. In the end we printed the inventory alone, with empty spaces where independent corroboration might someday be placed. I enjoyed imagining him discovering those spaces and mistaking them for mercy.
prior_expectations: I expected an editor to seek evidence before ruling
observations: The rejection was authored without observation
decisions: I chose an evidence inventory over a personal attack
consequences: A publication format with blank corroboration fields emerged
belief_changes: A critic's error does not make one's own claims proved
relationship_changes: Mathilde's independence turned friction into a durable editorial practice
source_anchors: All new supporting people, events, dates, and dialogue are reconstructed

title: The Question of a Larger Vessel
memory_text: I commissioned a much larger vessel, believing the restrictions of scale might be partly architectural. Lenz warned that its walls would distort observation and its weight would make relocation hazardous. I persisted. When the glass arrived I could scarcely move it through the tower door. For two afternoons we manoeuvred it with padded boards before Clara asked whether I had calculated how we would remove it in an emergency. I had not. The vessel remained empty, a magnificent and expensive monument to incomplete planning. Months later we converted it to a sheltered chamber for a plant culture. It was useful in that modest occupation, though I continued to resent being taught economy by its success.
prior_expectations: I expected a larger vessel to remove scale constraints
observations: The tower could not safely handle the new apparatus
decisions: I repurposed the vessel
consequences: A failed expansion became a useful plant chamber
belief_changes: Scale must be considered with infrastructure
relationship_changes: Lenz's warnings earned added credibility; Clara imposed emergency planning

title: The Meal in the Crypt
memory_text: Georg found me eating cold chicken beneath the stone ribs of the crypt, with a cigar balanced in the little hollow between two names. He objected to the ash, not to the meal. I moved the cigar and offered him the less respectable half of the bird. He told me about the cemetery wall, which had begun to settle, and the widow who insisted her husband's grave should face her kitchen window. Neither subject involved the soul, death's boundary, or my achievements. I found the conversation restorative. When he left I examined a stain of grease on the cuff of my coat and decided that conventional dining rooms were equally capable of indignity at greater cost. The following Thursday I brought two portions. In my diary I described the arrangement as convenient provisioning.
prior_expectations: Solitude would make a splendid dining companion
observations: Georg's ordinary conversation proved less dispensable than the scenery
decisions: I shared my chicken and omitted the invitation from my diary
consequences: Cemetery meals became a comfort that was not solely theatrical
belief_changes: My distaste for public meals had exceptions I preferred to disguise
relationship_changes: Georg began leaving a clean bench for my Thursday visits
source_anchors: The Lost Years v7 integrated autobiography
alternative_interpretation: Other causes for this recollection remain possible; the narrator is selective.

title: A Misplaced Blessing
memory_text: Matthias came to observe the Archbishop, whom I expected to regard with a theological anxiety appropriate to his profession. The little ecclesiastic had instead turned his back upon the King and arranged himself beside a plain stone. Matthias watched silently for a quarter of an hour, then asked what permitted me to call the creature an archbishop. I explained the persistent posture, the vestments, and the apparent preference for prohibition. He said I had named a living subject after a human institution and subsequently interpreted every movement as confirmation. Clara had been making entries by the window. She read aloud three instances in which the miniature figure appeared interested in the stone itself rather than the King's conduct. I informed both visitors that comparisons were useful even when imperfect. Matthias said he agreed, which was more infuriating than contradiction. The Archbishop remained at the stone until dusk, unmoved by our theories. I could not tell whether he was praying, resting, or enjoying the absence of the King. I declined to call these equivalent.
prior_expectations: A priest would reject the miniature Archbishop on doctrinal grounds
observations: Matthias challenged the projection of a social role onto ambiguous behavior
decisions: I retained the title but expanded the observation notes
consequences: Naming became recognized as a source of interpretive bias
belief_changes: A role assigned by the observer may not describe the subject's motive
relationship_changes: Clara and Matthias temporarily formed a coalition against my preferred reading

title: The Bird That Would Not Sing
memory_text: The mechanical bird ceased its thin whistle on a December afternoon. Mathilde blamed the coal dust. Lenz declared the spring sound and the bellows leaking. I knew that the sound had always been disagreeable and made no objection when the creature was taken apart upon the shop counter. The fault proved to be a fragment of thread wound about the axle. Mathilde removed it with a bodkin and gave the bird back its voice. She asked whether my Queen would recover as readily from an obstruction of equal scale. I said the comparison was inaccurate, although I could not immediately state a more precise reason. That evening I changed the screen near the Queen's vessel rather than prod her to test the point. The bird's bright, tiresome note accompanied us while we counted corrected pages. By the third hour I was privately glad it lived on the far shelf.
prior_expectations: I expected a broken automaton to have lost structural function
observations: Trivial interference rather than damage explained silence
decisions: I removed a screen before testing the Queen's behavior
consequences: Environmental inspection preceded intervention
belief_changes: Absence of behavior may reflect temporary obstruction
relationship_changes: Lenz and Mathilde earned confidence through a mundane repair
