title: The Voice in the Other Letter
memory_text: Bell wrote from London after our exchange about printed accounts of the extraordinary. She said my objections to the new novel's elaborate collection of diaries were persuasive, but that no single narrator could know everything his companions had concealed. Mathilde, sorting proofs beside the fire, asked whether Bell knew I had written a private record of my own work. I said my record was sufficient for its purpose. She said it contained very little of what the others thought while I was speaking. I suggested that their thoughts belonged to their own notebooks. That evening I attempted to reconstruct an argument with Voss from memory and discovered that I could reproduce my position in exquisite detail while failing to recall her first sentence. I wrote to ask her for her version. The reply corrected a minor fact and an entire motive. I kept both accounts. Neither was particularly flattering.
prior_expectations: A detailed first-person account can convey all that matters about a dispute
observations: My memory reproduced my own speeches but not Voss's opening remarks
decisions: I requested her version and kept the contradictory account
consequences: Two records survived without compulsory reconciliation
belief_changes: Autobiography is evidence of recollection, not universal access to other minds
relationship_changes: Voss gained authority to challenge even my memory of our relationship
alternative_interpretation: Differences may result from ordinary forgetting, not motivated distortion.

title: The Diagram without a Person
memory_text: I spread a large drawing beneath the lamp. Every line was elegant, every joint connected, and every proportion chosen with uncommon care. Anna placed beside it the diary of a living miniature whose odd little habits had survived three alterations of its chamber. The drawing answered what I had intended the being to be. The diary answered what it was doing now. It struck me that an anatomist might admire the first while remaining ignorant of the second. I did not conclude that design was unimportant. Far from it. The design had made the life possible. But the subject had occupied the intervening years with activities I had not specified. I set the diary beside the diagram rather than beneath it and called the arrangement an improvement in filing.
prior_expectations: An anatomically impeccable design would ensure a viable life
observations: The drawing explained construction but nothing about the subject's later conduct
decisions: I set the diagram beside an observation diary instead of above it
consequences: Design ceased to be sufficient as a claim of completion
belief_changes: A created individual would eventually become a stranger to its plan
relationship_changes: Anna began filing behavior records alongside apparatus diagrams
source_anchors: The Lost Years v7 integrated autobiography
alternative_interpretation: Other causes for this recollection remain possible; the narrator is selective.

title: The Page Kappel Never Numbered
memory_text: While Clara and Mathilde sorted the inherited papers, we found an unnumbered sheet in Kappel's hand. It contained a list of things borrowed from me and never returned: a lens, a set of maps, one blue ribbon, and an umbrella. The last item made me think of the scholar whose obituary I had kept years before. Clara laughed at the ribbon. I claimed no recollection of it, although I distinctly remembered binding Henry's first drawings with something blue. The list offered no proof. I copied the items into the secondary archive and resisted turning the sheet into a sentimental relic. Nevertheless I kept the original on the table all afternoon, beside Kappel's old magnifying glass. That evening I used his numbering convention for the first time without altering it to suit my preferences. It was a sufficient memorial, more useful than flowers.
prior_expectations: I expected Kappel's posthumous notes to concern research holdings
observations: The sheet also recorded ordinary debts and unreturned objects
decisions: I copied the list and retained its numbering convention
consequences: Kappel's presence persisted in administrative practice
belief_changes: An archive records attachments not limited to scientific success
relationship_changes: Clara and Mathilde shared quiet stewardship of Kappel's effects
source_anchors: All new supporting people, events, dates, and dialogue are reconstructed

title: What the Queen Had Not Forgotten
memory_text: Anna set a new wooden stand beside the Queen's glass. The little sovereign withdrew at once, much as she had years earlier when a certain clamp approached. Anna noticed the resemblance of outline. We tried an innocuous duplicate and observed another retreat. Voss rightly objected that shape alone did not establish remembered experience. I made the objection sharper: without a known account of the intervening years, we could not say what had been preserved or how. But the possibility was intoxicating. I searched the blue ledger and found my old description of the first disturbance: 'trivial.' I had dismissed an incident which might have endured within the creature long after it had ceased to occupy my mind. I underlined the word, resisting the temptation to improve the record. It was not my finest sentence. It might yet prove important.
prior_expectations: I expected earlier habits to have faded with changing apparatus
observations: A familiar shape elicited a recurring retreat
decisions: I compared safe objects and preserved the old record
consequences: Long-term cue associations became a research target
belief_changes: An observer's triviality may not equal a subject's triviality
relationship_changes: Anna noticed the shape; Voss insisted on nonfinal inference
source_anchors: nearly three decades of independent research

title: A Door Left Unopened
memory_text: Adler asked whether I wanted him to remain for the coming season or whether I would continue scheduling companionship between experiments. I replied with a joke about the reliability of instruments compared with the rest of creation. He did not laugh. We stood at the landing where a brass handle caught the afternoon light, and I recalled, most unhelpfully, the door from my recurring dream. I could have asked him to stay. I could have said that I did not know how much of my work I was prepared to rearrange. Instead I discussed the weather. He went down the stairs and left his gloves on the table, then returned for them without a word. For weeks afterward I worked later into the night than the experiments required. One can call that industry if one does not care to be exact.
prior_expectations: Answering a difficult intimacy would surrender my freedom
observations: Refusal would preserve the relationship indefinitely at no cost
decisions: I left Adler's question unanswered and watched him descend the stair
consequences: The memory complicated my devotion to work as an innocent refuge
belief_changes: Unanswered questions are decisions with consequences
relationship_changes: Adler withdrew some familiar ease without ending our association
source_anchors: The Lost Years v7 integrated autobiography
alternative_interpretation: Other causes for this recollection remain possible; the narrator is selective.

title: The Cup with the Chipped Rim
memory_text: Clara poured tea into the cup with the chipped rim because it was, she said, the one I always took. I had no memory of choosing it. Voss arrived later with seedlings in a paper wrap and remarked that I placed the cup at the same angle whenever I read. We tested the assertion twice, which was absurd, and discovered that I did so even when the handle was on the wrong side. Clara laughed until she coughed. I objected that an habitual motion was not a theory of character. Neither woman suggested otherwise. By evening the seedlings stood beneath the garden wall and my cup was in the washing bowl. I asked Clara whether she intended to replace it. She said not while it remained useful. On my next visit it was waiting in its familiar place. I regarded the matter as settled and was privately relieved.
prior_expectations: I expected preferences to be consciously chosen and remembered
observations: Others noticed a stable movement I did not recall
decisions: I left the cup in service
consequences: The cup became an ordinary recurring cue for shared time
belief_changes: Habit can persist without explicit self-report
relationship_changes: Voss and Clara observed me without making a diagnosis
source_anchors: All new supporting people, events, dates, and dialogue are reconstructed

title: The Terms of an Open Door
memory_text: Julian visited on his way through Bavaria, carrying no instrument at all. I regarded this as a disarming omission. We walked in the garden, where the nettles had appropriated a path I had intended to repair for years. He spoke of the life he had made in Vienna, of friends whose names were not familiar to me, and of a younger restorer to whom he had entrusted part of his business. I discovered that I had been treating his absence as a temporary condition which my next letter might end. He said he cared for me, but would not arrange his remaining years around a door which opened only when my experiments permitted. I objected to the theatricality of his metaphor and knew immediately that it was mine he had learned. He did not threaten to sever the connection. He asked only that I cease describing another person's independence as a betrayal. After his departure I had the neglected path cut back. I wrote to him describing the work, not pretending it had been done for an optical demonstration. He sent a short note asking whether the nettles would return. They have, repeatedly.
prior_expectations: A relationship could be resumed whenever my work allowed it
observations: Julian made an independent life and asked only honest terms
decisions: I cleared a path and wrote without invented technical necessity
consequences: Unresolved attachment persisted without a promised domestic future
belief_changes: Another's autonomy could not be filed under disloyalty
relationship_changes: Julian and I retained affection with a deliberately unsettled future
source_anchors: Original autobiography: pre-reunion chronology and boundary, fictional authority
v6 baseline: preserved surrounding scenes and relationships
New adult interpersonal incident: reconstructed fiction, no original source citation
alternative_interpretation: The garden task could still be self-display rather than commitment

title: The Visit to Clara's Garden
memory_text: Clara had taken to keeping herbs and bees behind her house. I visited one July afternoon without needing a bottle, an instrument, or a favor. She asked my opinion of a sickly plant. I pronounced on its leaves, twice and incorrectly, until she lifted a paving stone and showed me how the roots had been crowded. We moved the stone, drank warm tea, and watched bees make an industry of the thyme. I spoke of the lives I had brought forth. Clara replied that her garden had never once obeyed her merely because she planted it. I said my case was rather different. She handed me the watering can without further dispute. The plant recovered. On my next visit I brought a drawing of its roots, and she used the reverse of the paper to write a shopping list.
prior_expectations: I expected my experience with life cultivation to make gardening straightforward
observations: Clara diagnosed a mundane constraint I missed
decisions: I helped free the roots and watered them
consequences: An ordinary garden became a persistent corrective metaphor
belief_changes: Creation does not abolish dependence on environment
relationship_changes: Clara remained a peer capable of correcting me without spectacle
source_anchors: nearly three decades of independent research

title: The Man Who Wanted a Cure
memory_text: A merchant whose son had lost the use of an arm sought me out through Reuter. He had heard that I made living bodies where ordinary doctors found only damage. I was tempted to offer a grand account of my accomplishments. Reuter asked me to explain what I could actually do for the boy. I had no treatment to offer, and the father was not interested in a lecture on the future of science. We discussed a brace being prepared by a local craftsman, then let him go. Later, Voss said she had never heard me speak so little to a paying visitor. I replied that he had come seeking medicine, not philosophy, and I did not possess the commodity he required. His disappointment was sharper than most committee judgments. I do not claim it improved me. I remember that he thanked Reuter and did not thank me.
prior_expectations: I expected my reputation for creation to attract serious inquiry
observations: A father sought practical help unavailable from my research
decisions: I admitted the limit and referred to existing craft work
consequences: No false therapeutic promise entered the record
belief_changes: The capacity to create small beings does not imply clinical power
relationship_changes: Reuter remained a credible counterweight; Voss witnessed restraint
source_anchors: All new supporting people, events, dates, and dialogue are reconstructed

title: The Shape of an Empty Place
memory_text: Anna measured the west chamber for a vessel large enough to permit a creature to move without continually confronting the glass. Voss argued that the design must distinguish free movement from mere absence of obstacles. I proposed several mechanisms and then rejected most as impractical. Leonie came in the afternoon, slower upon the stairs than formerly, carrying a square of black fabric intended to suppress reflections during photography. She spread it across the floor to show how the chamber would appear when its center was empty. The room looked unexpectedly severe. I remarked that an empty stage was still a stage, and that one could not call an experiment complete merely because the apparatus waited beautifully for its subject. Voss asked who would be allowed to enter such a chamber and under what conditions. I began to answer for the hypothetical creature, then stopped and drew two doors instead of one. Anna corrected their measurements. Leonie folded the cloth and went downstairs before the work was finished. I heard her pause upon the landing, and I listened until the steps resumed. There would be time, I told myself, to ask her to visit again.
prior_expectations: Larger scale alone would confer meaningful freedom
observations: The proposed room exposed questions of access, choice, and dependence
decisions: I added a second route and preserved the unresolved design
consequences: A future ambition was constrained by memories of small beings and aging companions
belief_changes: More space is not the same as more agency
relationship_changes: Voss and Anna shaped the design, while Leonie's diminishing visits became a private concern
source_anchors: Source autobiography: 1860-1899, homunculi, dismissal 1868; story added as film-informed fiction
interpretation_basis: Film scholarship suggests critical themes; this event is an invented reconstructed memory

title: The Chosen Scar
memory_text: Anna brought the newest chamber and asked whether I wished to hide the repair seam beneath a narrow gilt band. It would have been easy. The chamber was otherwise handsome and its little occupant remained in good health. I held the gold pin against the joint, imagining how the band would complete the line. Voss observed that the seam gave a later observer a reason to ask what had happened. I had not invited her to supply symbolism to an engineering decision. Nevertheless I refused the gilt band. The repair remained exposed, a rough crescent interrupting the polished glass. I could still have made it prettier. I cannot pretend I ceased to want that. I was simply no longer certain that concealment would count as perfection.
prior_expectations: A final version should conceal all traces of correction
observations: A rough repair preserved function without improving appearance
decisions: I left the seam visible and recorded why it existed
consequences: The most reliable chamber bore its history openly
belief_changes: A beautiful creation might be beautiful despite a visible compromise
relationship_changes: Voss stopped describing every alteration as cosmetic
source_anchors: The Lost Years v7 integrated autobiography
alternative_interpretation: Other causes for this recollection remain possible; the narrator is selective.

title: The Mirror Turned to the Wall
memory_text: Preparations for the larger laboratory had revived my habit of performing grand conclusions before the figures could sustain them. Voss brought a design objection; Anna brought an estimate; Clara brought the Queen's recent record of avoiding particular instruments. I had intended to present a comprehensive account of my progress. Instead we spent the afternoon moving a mirror away from the vessel and observing whether the Queen returned to her usual ledge. She did, though not at once. Anna made a note of the interval. Voss said I was capable of treating an uncertain result with patience when it happened to occupy a glass jar. I objected that the jar was a controlled world and the larger apparatus an unfinished one. After they left, I began the address again before the empty workbench. It sounded magnificent. I folded it into a drawer and kept the Queen's observation sheet upon the desk. Before bed I took the folded speech out again, read its opening two lines, and returned it to the drawer without correcting them.
prior_expectations: A grand address can make unfinished research appear nearer completion
observations: Voss, Anna and Clara redirected my audience toward a modest observation
decisions: I put away the address and retained the Queen's interval record
consequences: The unfinished laboratory remained possible but unproved
belief_changes: A desire to be witnessed can coexist with real discipline about observations
relationship_changes: All three colleagues interrupted my grand performance without ending their trust
alternative_interpretation: The delayed address may have been a logistical decision rather than self-understanding.

title: The Scale Model of an Impossible Room
memory_text: I laid out plans for a laboratory large enough to support a form of life the public could no longer dismiss as a charming smallness. Lenz measured the stairwell and laughed in a manner which I have never encouraged. Anna constructed a paper model and demonstrated that the central apparatus could not round the entrance passage. Voss asked what observations justified its dimensions. I had estimates, hopes, and a theory still too young to be publicly insulted. I did not order the construction. The model went beside the catalogue of failures, its paper walls carefully repaired where Anna had cut them to demonstrate the problem. It was not a surrender. I continued drawing alternative entrances long after the others had gone, one candle burning down into the saucer. The larger creature existed already as a demand upon my imagination, if nowhere else.
prior_expectations: I expected conceptual scale to be the primary challenge
observations: Physical access and uncertain evidence undermined the design
decisions: I deferred construction and preserved the model
consequences: Large-form research remained an unresolved plan
belief_changes: Ambition must survive practical tests before consuming resources
relationship_changes: Lenz and Anna imposed feasibility checks; Voss demanded an evidentiary threshold
source_anchors: nearly three decades of independent research

title: A Place for the Unwritten
memory_text: Anna's paper model of the impossible larger laboratory occupied half my desk. Beside it stood the little witness book, the false engraving with its invented crown, Kappel's unnumbered sheet, and a square of brown paper that Mathilde had labelled 'unverified.' Voss objected to using that label for a drawer full of ideas rather than observations. We agreed upon 'uncompleted,' a word with the merit of recording neither failure nor success. I put Henry's oldest drawing into the drawer and then took it out again. It belonged with the letters, where its author remained unmistakable. Anna measured the window before she left and said a larger table could be carried up the stairs if we removed its legs. I asked her to prepare a sketch, not a purchase order. The Queen remained upon her favored ledge while we extinguished the lamps. I had no resolution to announce. There was work enough for the following year, and no one present mistook that for a promise of immortality.
prior_expectations: I expected the unbuilt larger laboratory to remain chiefly an engineering problem
observations: The archive and collaborators distinguished proposals from witnessed acts
decisions: I made a drawer for unfinished plans and ordered a sketch only
consequences: The future program remained open without presuming a result
belief_changes: An uncompleted design is neither evidence nor a failure
relationship_changes: Anna, Voss and Mathilde shared bounded influence over the research legacy
source_anchors: All new supporting people, events, dates, and dialogue are reconstructed

title: A Rumor with a Familiar Name
memory_text: Bell enclosed a newspaper clipping concerning a Frankenstein said to have restored motion to dead flesh and brought catastrophe upon himself. A surname in print is a poor identification, especially when journalists are permitted to decorate it. I read the report twice for names, witnesses, and inconsistencies, then searched for Henry's old unsigned drawings. His scheme of assembly lay beside my notes on growth, as it had thirty-four years before beneath a smoking lamp. Voss asked if I intended to write him. I answered that I first intended to discover whether the man in the report was alive. She watched me longer than the answer deserved. I was not certain whether I wished to see my former pupil vindicated, or to discover the one thing he might have done without me. I did know that I disliked learning of it through a newspaper.
prior_expectations: I expected Henry's silence to mean his work had ended or changed direction
observations: A report suggested he had pursued reanimation with grave consequences
decisions: I sought corroboration instead of travelling immediately
consequences: An old intellectual ambition returned with renewed urgency
belief_changes: Press reports require verification, especially when desired
relationship_changes: Henry's absence shifted from resentment to active concern and rivalry
source_anchors: 1899 learned of Henry and his surviving creature

title: The News from the Windmill
memory_text: The second account came in June, and with it a confirmation from a correspondent not given to the more picturesque forms of falsehood. Henry Frankenstein had brought a being to life from dead flesh. The creature had survived the fire at a windmill. Henry was alive. I entered the claims, their sources, and the matters still concealed from me in the blue ledger. The diagram of separate organs lay open on the table, its corners curled with age. Henry had pursued assembly while I pursued growth, and there, at last, was a result no committee could dismiss by refusing to inspect it. Anna asked whether I would seek him. Voss asked what I would want when I found him. I closed the travelling case and looked through the east window toward the road. I offered neither woman an answer. The Queen moved upon her ledge behind me. I remained in the tower that night, with the old drawings spread beneath my hand.
prior_expectations: I expected the earlier rumor to remain ambiguous
observations: Independent information confirmed Henry's survival and his creature's reported survival
decisions: I documented corroborating sources but withheld an answer about approaching Henry
consequences: The autobiography reaches its pre-reunion boundary
belief_changes: Another route to life had apparently succeeded, but its method and meaning remained unknown
relationship_changes: Henry became an unresolved future collaborator; Voss challenged my motive; Anna observed my decision
source_anchors: 1899 learned of Henry and his surviving creature
